Now, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva’s *Verses on the Immeasurable Life* already states that there are twenty-four chapters of vows; such was the ancient manuscript from the Western Regions.
Therefore, the two earlier translations—the Han and Wu versions—followed this as twenty-four vows, whereas the Wei translation [established the forty-eight].
The text is redundant and repetitive; its earlier and later sections are identical.

For this reason, the Tang translation abridged it to forty-six vows, and the Song translation further abridged it to thirty-four vows. Thus, it did not circulate in antiquity, nor does it circulate today.

To sentient beings, it appears as a pit of earth, stones, and rubble; yet when the World-Honored One exercises his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he transforms the ground so that it becomes entirely a precious ground of lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*).

These are different sensations. There are no sentient beings who do not possess the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Possessing the six sense organs, they necessarily possess the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Therefore, the eyes desire to exhaust all colors in the world; the ears desire to exhaust all sounds in the world; the tongue desires to exhaust all flavors in the world;

Contact. The mind desires the most delightful things in the world. Those who seek and obtain them receive the karmic rewards of the various heavens;

In the human realm, one is enslaved for a lifetime by the physical body, wife, and children; suffering and pleasure are half-and-half. Furthermore, wealth and status drown a person; it is easy [to be lost].
One enters the three miserable realms. Such are the difficulties of the householder. As for those who have left the home life as monks, regarding the two gates of doctrine and practice:

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
Together with twelve hundred and fifty people, all of whom were great śrāvakas well-known to the assembly. Their names were:

Virtue. Exercising skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they travel through the lands of all Buddhas, universally manifesting themselves everywhere to make offerings to all Buddhas and to transform and guide sentient beings.

They penetrate the characteristics of sentient beings and comprehend the nature of all phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*). This is like a skilled illusionist who conjures the forms of men, women, and so forth;

He maintains immeasurable hundreds of thousands of samādhis and dwells in the gates of profound meditative concentration.

He beholds all the immeasurable Buddhas of the present and, within a single thought-moment, travels throughout all Buddha-lands. He discerns the languages of sentient beings and regards them with compassion as if they were his own kin.
Vowing to accomplish the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas, he transcends the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu...

It surpasses the merit of the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas below, as well as that of all devas, humans, and the myriad classes of crawling and flying creatures accumulated through giving over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. Why is this? Because it concerns all future devas, humans, and every sentient being.

There was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata. He remained in the world for forty-two kalpas.

Within that Buddha’s Dharma, there was a bhikṣu named Dharmākara, who had originally been a king. Having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, he immediately conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment.
He abandoned his kingdom and renounced his royal status to become a śramaṇa; his wisdom and valor were such that none could surpass him.
He approached the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, I have already resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
I pray that the Buddha will extensively proclaim for me the adornments of the pure lands of all Buddhas, so that I may attain peerless awakening in this world and achieve great bodhi. At that time...
The Buddha Sovereign King said to the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, "As for the adornment of Buddha-lands, you should take them up yourself.
The Bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying, "This meaning is vast and profound; it is not within my domain. I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound it for me.
At that time, the Buddha Sovereign King, knowing his high intelligence and his deep and broad aspirations, immediately expounded for him at length two hundred and ten [vows].
He manifested before them all the billions of Buddha-fields, the good and evil of devas and humans, and the coarse and sublime of their lands, appearing exactly according to their mental aspirations.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu beheld all those purified lands and gave rise to unsurpassed, most excellent vows;
his mind became tranquil, his will was free from attachment, and he cultivated merit while making great oaths.
He made this vow: "I wish to gather and adorn [merits] for the full duration of five kalpas. Having gone before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, I said:

'Now, for the sake of the bodhisattva path, I desire that when I later become a buddha, my wisdom, radiance, and merit shall be preeminent among all the countless buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, surpassing those of all other buddha-fields. Is this possible? The Buddha said: 'It is like this...'"

It is like the great ocean: even if a single person were to measure it with a peck-measure throughout the course of kalpas, its bottom might still be reached; if a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart, what wish could they not attain?

At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and stood with palms joined, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, I have already taken up the pure practices for adorning Buddha-lands; may you deign to hear and examine them. First Vow:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be no three evil realms within my land—should there be hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals—even those who merely hear their names shall not attain true enlightenment. Second Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land...”
They shall be born solely by transformation; there shall be no birth from a womb, nor shall there be women.

Should women from other lands wish to be reborn in my land, at the end of their lives they shall immediately manifest as male bodies and come to my buddha-field, being born within lotus flowers. Only when the flowers open shall they behold the Buddha.
If this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the third vow. Furthermore, if upon my becoming a Buddha, the devas and humans in my land...

Fourth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are differences in physical form and appearance such that they are not all golden in color and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, if the devas and humans in my land do not all possess the knowledge of past lives, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Fifth Vow: "I shall not attain perfect enlightenment unless, upon my becoming a Buddha, the devas and humans in my land do not obtain the divine eye, at least to see hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands.
Sixth Vow: "I shall not attain perfect enlightenment unless, upon my becoming a Buddha, the devas and humans in my land..."

If, upon attaining Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not obtain the divine ear—such that they cannot hear and fully retain everything spoken by as many as hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas—I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the seventh vow. Furthermore, if, upon attaining Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not obtain the knowledge of others' minds—such that they cannot know even as many as hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of beings within the lands of various Buddhas—I shall not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the eighth vow.

If, upon conceiving this thought, I do not attain perfect enlightenment—this is my eighth vow. Furthermore, if, when I have attained Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land are unable to exercise spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) such that, in a single moment of thought, they cannot travel at least past hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayutas* of Buddha-lands—then may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
This is my ninth vow. Furthermore, if, when I have attained Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land...

Tenth Vow: I shall not attain perfect enlightenment if, when I have become a Buddha, the gods and humans in my land do not all obtain a broad and long tongue, and are not skillful in preaching the Dharma with unimpeded eloquence.
Eleventh Vow: I shall not attain perfect enlightenment if, when I have become a Buddha, my light...

If, when I have attained...
"O Buddha, if my lifespan should have a limit, even as short as a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the thirteenth vow. Furthermore, if upon my attaining Buddhahood, the śrāvakas in my land should have a measurable number—even if all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to become pratyekabuddhas and together calculate their number for a hundred thousand kalpas—[may I not attain perfect enlightenment]."
If, upon knowing their number, I do not attain perfect enlightenment—this is the fourteenth vow.

Furthermore, if, when I have attained Buddhahood, the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land is likewise equal to that of the Buddha, being immeasurable and forever free from birth and death—except for those who, by their original vows, manifest mastery over long or short lifespans—if it were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment—this is the fifteenth vow. Furthermore, if, when I have attained Buddhahood...

Sixteenth Vow: If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, the gods and humans within my land do not all possess boundless radiance that illuminates the Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, if my fame and renown do not spread universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Seventeenth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the innumerable Buddhas do not all praise and extol my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, if sentient beings in the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should resolve their minds on Bodhi and, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land—even if they should, at the moment of death, seek rebirth there with ten recitations—if they do not see me and the great [assembly], may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

I shall not attain perfect enlightenment until I appear before that person, surrounded by a multitude [of followers], except in the case of those who have committed the five heinous crimes or have slandered the true Dharma.
(The Eighteenth Vow): "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from the various Buddha-lands of other directions do not come to be born in my land..."
Ultimately, they shall surely reach the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

Except for those who, by the power of their original vows, freely transform sentient beings, they shall travel throughout all Buddha-lands to practice the bodhisattva path for the sake of liberating all beings.

Although they may be born in other lands, they shall never undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms, and their roots of goodness shall never regress or be lost. If it were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the nineteenth [vow].

Vow Twenty: If, when I have attained Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land—though they may abide in the stages of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—are unable to receive the Buddha’s spiritual power and make offerings to all Buddhas for even the duration of a single meal, or if they cannot travel everywhere to innumerable and immeasurable Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

During the Tongzhi era, my late father, Master Meishu, once remarked: "Wei’s edition of the scriptural text is sufficient to serve as the crown for all the Mahāyāna sūtras."

regarding the name of the Buddha in the sutra, it is sometimes rendered as "Immeasurable Life" and sometimes as "Amitābha"; this has already been explained in detail in the preceding examples.

Furthermore, there are other textual passages that still require discussion; thus, I have extensively examined various editions and personally collated them by hand.

Consequently, Gengxin was able to thoroughly examine the various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, whereby he came to realize that the subtle words of the Ultimate Way are fundamentally not something that can be understood through conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Yet, the entire world remains in a state of dreamy delusion, inverting right and wrong.

This was by no means the merit of those within the six realms of existence or the heavens and humans. Thereafter, having personally encountered the entanglements of the world, he did not wish to incur the reproach of occupying a position while his words remained loftily detached.

He maintained himself in silence, using his words only to decline invitations and avoid illness. This has now been more than twenty years. Lately, as his years approach their twilight, he has grown apprehensive about his own physical decline;
moreover, he currently faces many hardships within the state, where heterodox doctrines run rampant, whether from Confucians or Buddhists, leaving little room for respite.
At the place where the Emperor was stationed, he remained awake throughout the night, his hidden anxieties pressing upon him with urgency.

He then took the copies of the scriptures collated by his late father and appended to them several tens of thousands of words of his own reflections to show to future students. His writing draws upward from the vehicles of the teachings and pours forth downward from his own realization of the mind.

To bring forth the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one must not merely indulge in empty talk. Therefore, this sutra and this treatise are neither identical nor different, yet they are both identical and different.

This meaning is set forth as the text; furthermore, it concludes with occasional questions. That which is detailed in the sutra is abbreviated here; that which is abbreviated in the sutra is detailed here.

The essential purport of this school likewise cannot be fully set forth; moreover, it provides no means to synthesize the various schools as the fundamental root of the Ultimate Way.
Alas! The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift. How could this be something entrusted to empty words while remaining oblivious to practical efficacy?
How could one fully comprehend it? The aspirations of sages lie in transcending the world. If you wish to take the highest as your model, do not neglect this.

There are two realities regarding birth and death: the first is called *paricchinna-janma-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death), and the second is called *pariṇāmi-janma-maraṇa* (transformative birth and death). Segmented...
Regarding birth and death: the conjunction of the four great elements is called birth; the dispersal of the four great elements is called death.

This refers to the birth and death within the cycle of the six realms. Regarding the birth and death of transformation: when the cause shifts and the fruit changes, transforming the coarse into the subtle, it is called birth;

when one abandons the position currently occupied, it is called death. This refers to the birth and death of advancing toward the One Vehicle. As for the birth and death of segmented divisions: [the text continues as follows:]... [segmented division] birth and death.
There is the birth-and-death of inherent birth-and-death, and the birth-and-death of transformation. There is also the birth-and-death of that which is fundamentally without birth-and-death;
because the saving of sentient beings is never-ending, one enters the realms by means of the great compassionate vow, and thus this too is conventionally designated as "birth-and-death."
To still be stalled in the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) is to be within the realm; this refers to the six classes of ordinary beings.

To have already realized the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa*) is to be outside the realm; this refers to the true fruits of the four noble ones. To remain stalled within the realm is to dwell in the world.

To have already transcended the boundaries of the realms is what constitutes "transcending the world. Within the six classes of ordinary beings in the realm, there is only the pursuit of birth and extinction:

using fundamental emotions to create karma, and using fundamental karma to undergo rebirth. Thus they cycle through the six paths, sometimes flourishing and sometimes withering, sometimes suffering and sometimes joyful.
Yet, in the end, there is no real happiness upon which one can rely. If one cannot advance toward True Suchness (*tathatā*), their suffering and exhaustion will never come to an end.
Therefore, it is said that while ordinary beings undergo birth and death, the four types of noble ones (*ārya*) outside the realm of desire realize True Suchness through partial realization.

With their fundamental nature as the path for advancement, they all ride upon great compassion and vast vows to roam freely within the three realms to rescue and deliver sentient beings. Their coming...

It must have a purpose. Its progression must have a realization. This continues until the tenth stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), reaching the ultimate pinnacle of Unsurpassed Perfect Complete Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) before coming to rest.
Therefore it is said: "Birth and death that are fundamentally non-existent" and "birth and death that are inherently existent" involve ascent and descent;
yet one ascends but once and descends nine times. Even if one reaches birth in the heavens, one still cannot transcend them.
Beyond the realm of segmented existence—that which is called the suffering of saṃsāra—is this very state. It is a birth-and-death that is fundamentally non-existent;

there is ascent but no descent, movement and stillness are free, and one always progresses further upward. Because this birth-and-death exists solely for the purpose of delivering sentient beings and fulfilling vows, it cannot be discussed in the same terms as ordinary birth-and-death.
Having already transcended the bounds of birth-and-death, one nevertheless enters into birth-and-death.
Those who, within the realm of the world, deliver sentient beings are called Bodhisattvas; this is the Mahāyāna.

Having transcended the bounds of birth and death, they subsequently realize a semblance of nirvāṇa—neither arising nor ceasing—and seek only their own solitary perfection, no longer maintaining the intention to deliver sentient beings;
these are called Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the two vehicles of the Small and Middling [Vehicles]. As for these two vehicles of the Small and Middling...

They are rebuked by all the Buddhas because they lack the intention to deliver sentient beings; this clearly contradicts the Mahāyāna, as such individuals will certainly be unable to advance to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Transformation-death (pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa) is like a wise and noble official being promoted: although there is a change of position, [the essence remains].

Each time they advance toward the higher realms, their segmented birth and death (paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa) is like a refugee seeking food; there is immediate fluctuation between prosperity and decline, yet ultimately there is no foundation for stability.

When one thoroughly examines the ultimate state of the ten realms, it is only the Buddhas of the One Vehicle who eternally realize the bliss of nirvana, while it is only the sentient beings within the six paths who perpetually suffer the calamities of saṃsāra. The cycle of sentient beings...
[Response: Although there are distinctions among the six realms of existence, human existence must necessarily be regarded as the pivotal point.

Among sentient beings in the human realm, those who accumulate virtuous karma are not even one or two in a hundred; those who accumulate evil karma exceed the sands of the Ganges in number. Even speaking only in terms of virtuous karma:
If one is unable to cultivate supramundane merit and wisdom, but merely accumulates mundane causes of goodness, the ultimate limit of such practice will not exceed rebirth in the heavens.
Although the lifespan in the heavenly realms is long and their karmic rewards are superior, they ultimately remain within the confines of birth-and-death characterized by fragmentation.
Once the retribution of merit is exhausted, one must inevitably fall into decline. Having fallen, the calamities of the three miserable realms can ultimately not be avoided.
Such is the way of the heavenly realm; the other realms may be known by this. Such is the nature of wholesome karma; unwholesome karma may be known by this.
Those who possess neither good nor evil karma may likewise be known by this. Therefore, for all those who cannot transcend the three realms, regardless of their station—
Regarding good and evil, the calamities of the three miserable realms cannot be transcended with ease and freedom from entanglement. Having been born, one dies again; having died, one is born again.
Birth must have its origin, and death must have its destination. Birth and death entwine one another, and their ultimate limit is unknown.
Even if one cultivates the fruits of goodness, one will not fail to remain on the path of virtue for at most one or two lifetimes. Should one falter even slightly, one will once more fall into ruin.

Indeed, with the limited illumination of a single crack in the conditioned world, the mind cannot withstand the thickness of beginningless karmic habituation. This is an inevitable force and an inherent principle;
it is not to be wondered at. What is called "understanding birth and death" refers precisely to understanding this birth and death of the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm;
what is called "liberation from birth and death" refers precisely to liberation from this birth and death of the *pariccheda* realm alone. And...
Sentient beings within the realms, because they do not understand the two types of birth-and-death, do not know the method for cultivation and realization.
Since they do not understand the method for cultivation and realization, those of superior capacity do no more than delineate the great void and open up their own gateways.

Thus they establish their learning for abiding in the world. Those of lower capacity inevitably become stubbornly attached to deluded karma and strive with forceful competition within the three miserable realms.

Those of higher capacity may ascend, yet achieve nothing more than superficial joy; those of lower capacity descend, eventually harboring deep sorrow. Thus, through kalpas upon kalpas, all remains vast and boundless in confusion.
We have all together sunk into the long night; those whom the Buddhas call "objects of pity" are precisely these people—how tragic this is!
Indeed, to conceal one’s illness and dread medical treatment is truly a cause for alarm and wonder.

To do so while still in the prime of youth and vigor is to suddenly mock Jivaka and Bian Que, failing to realize that even a person in their prime will eventually face a day of decline and sickness. Though the outcomes differ, the delusion is no different. O worthy ones!
If a wise person possesses true knowledge, how could they fail to understand how to conduct themselves regarding the causes of birth and death and the source of the Great Way?

The various devas of the three realms, down to those in the hells, are the domain of *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death).
The ascent and descent through the six paths of existence are the fruit of *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*. The twelve classes of living beings are the manifestations of *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*.

Whether ascending or descending, the cycle of rebirth continues without ceasing; this is the perilous nature of *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*. Once fallen into the three miserable paths, one remains there for aeons.
Kalpas. The karmic power of sentient beings is inconceivable. The cruelty of the hells and the submerged suffering of the hungry ghosts and animals are likewise inconceivable;

Having passed through the prison of the womb time and again without complaint, and having repeatedly changed masks without shame, though one might wish to return directly to annihilation, one does not know that fundamentally there is no such thing as annihilation, nor is there any principle of annihilation. being born and dying moment by moment, one can never attain freedom, nor will one ever be willing to attain freedom from this segmented birth-and-death.

Moreover, they ultimately refuse to seek their own liberation from it; some even go so far as to harbor a deep aversion toward the Great Sages who have transcended the world and who hope for others' liberation.

It is simply this: these are the ones for whom the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas feel compassion; these are the ones they contemplate.

Yet, when these people hear what is not heard, see what is not seen, or know what is not known, they turn red in the face, point their fingers in anger, and slander incessantly, even exerting all their strength to reject the Great [Teaching] that transcends the world.

In seeking to penetrate the causes of birth and death, one must first understand the measure of space (*dharmadhātu*), and next, the measure of the mind.
