Therefore, there is currently no means by which to penetrate this; some may even pass through kalpas without knowing why it is so, ultimately ending in spiritual decline and ruin—how lamentable!
The mind-measure (*citta-mātra*) is the source, while the phenomenal world (*bhāva-mātra*) is the flow. The mind-measure is the cause, while the phenomenal world is the effect.

Nevertheless, regarding the doctrine of the mind-measure, if one draws analogies from within one's own person, those who possess even a slight degree of supramundane insight may be able to understand it.
Regarding the discourse on dimensions and measurements, many consider it beyond the reach of the ears and eyes, and none fail to suspect it as absurdity.
Some regard it as a mere allegory from the works of Zhuangzi and Liezi, unaware that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment have already fully realized True Suchness (Tathatā).
Consequently, they are able to penetrate its principles everywhere and traverse its realms everywhere, thereby revealing them to sentient beings without sparing their own refinement.
All those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas compassionately regard sentient beings and transform them for their deliverance; they are as busy as the sun has no leisure.
How could they deign to direct their efforts toward the likes of childish insects and falsely compose parables that result only in frivolous discourse?

Yet, those who are greatly deluded do not understand until the end of their lives, and those who are not foolish do not become enlightened until the end of their lives; every time they hold this view, it serves as an obstacle.

If the provisions for the Path as set forth in the fundamental scriptures were to remain largely unestablished, then to propagate the essential principles of the dimensions [of the universe] in order to dispel delusions and confusion is truly what the Buddhas of the past would have deeply approved. What, then, are these dimensions?

Within the Dharma-realm there are ten, which are collectively divided into four lands. As for the ten realms: first, the Buddha realm; second, the Bodhisattva realm; third, the Pratyekabuddha realm; [and so on].
1. The realm of śrāvakas; 2. the realm of devas; 3. the realm of humans; 4. the realm of asuras; 5. the realm of animals; 6. the realm of hungry ghosts; 7.
the realm of hell-dwellers. Regarding the four lands: first is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, where all Buddhas reside;
second is the Land of True Reward Adornment, where bodhisattvas of the ten stages reside; third is the Land of Expedient Means...
The remaining lands are those inhabited by *pratyekabuddhas* and *śrāvakas*. The fourth is called the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages;

it is the dwelling place of various sages who have manifested their retribution, as well as sentient beings from the heavenly beings downward. From the various heavens down to the hells, these are collectively termed the Three Realms (*tridhātu*) and also called the Six Paths (*ṣadgati*).
Heavenly beings, humans, and *asuras* constitute the paths of goodness, while animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings constitute the paths of suffering.

The three evil realms (*durgati*) and the three good realms (*sugati*) are the places where sentient beings with virtuous karma take birth. The three evil realms are also called the "three paths" (*trivartman*);

these are all places where sentient beings with evil karma fall and descend. The three realms (*tridhātu*) are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
From the hells upward, reaching as far as the six heavens of the desire realm, they are collectively designated as the realm of desire, because they all possess...

These are the passions of men and women. From the six heavens of desire upward, as one ascends successively, there are further the three heavens of the first dhyāna, the three heavens of the second dhyāna, the three heavens of the third dhyāna, and the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna; these collectively constitute the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).

Because they possess only the physical body and are entirely devoid of the passions of men and women, [they are so named]. From the heavens of the Realm of Form upward, as one ascends successively, there are further...

There are four heavens of emptiness (*ākāśa*), which together constitute the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Because they all lack physical bodies and possess only spirit and consciousness, they are like ghosts and spirits.
This constitutes the twenty-eight heavens of the Three Realms. Below the six heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are further three heavens that dwell upon the earth;
ascending successively from these, there is one heaven that dwells in space. Above the heavens dwelling in space is the [upper portion] of the Desire Realm.
This is the first heaven. These constitute the thirty-two heavens of the triple world (*tridhātu*), which comprise the entirety of the celestial realms.
The names of these heavens are recorded in detail in such scriptures as the *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-śūraṅgama-sūtra* and others; they shall not be described here in full. There are four types of *asura*s:

some are subsumed within the realm of humans (*manuṣya-gati*), some within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*), and some within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni-gati*). Only the *asura* kings maintain [their distinct status].
The World of Power, Penetration, Fearlessness, and Ability to Compete for Authority with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.

They cultivate only celestial merit and do not cultivate celestial wisdom. Their dwelling places are adjacent to the sun and moon; they serve as vassals to the heavens and are therefore subsumed within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*).
Nevertheless, they may also be established as a distinct world (*dhātu*). There are also the realms of Quiescent Light, True Reward, and Expedient Means.
The other three lands constitute the four realms of the noble ones (*ārya*), as they are all inhabited by supramundane sages.

From the devas and humans down to the hells, these constitute the six realms of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Although it is said that ordinary beings and sages dwell together [in these lands], because the sages reside there only as temporary manifestations of their retribution, they are still referred to as the "six realms of ordinary beings.
Within this Sahā world of cohabitation, there are two categories each for both ordinary beings and sages. Regarding the two types of ordinary beings, the first is...

"Evil sentient beings" refers to those of the four realms of existence (*caturgati*). "Virtuous sentient beings" refers to humans and devas. The four realms of existence consist of the three miserable paths (*tridurgati*) and the asuras;
because asuras possess celestial merit but lack celestial virtue, they are also termed an evil realm. Regarding the two types of sages:

first are the true sages, namely those of the four fruits, pratyekabuddhas, those at the sixth stage of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna*), those at the ten abodes of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi*), and those in the ten stages of faith of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).
In the latter case, although the delusions have been exhausted through the penetration of the mind, the retribution body (*vipākakāya*) still remains; these are all termed "real.

Second are the provisional sages (*upāyika-ārya*), which refers to the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas of Wondrous Enlightenment within the three lands of the Land of Tranquil Light, the Land of Real Reward, and the Land of Expedient Means.

To deliver sentient beings with whom they have a karmic affinity, they manifest in the Land of Common Residence; these are all considered "provisional. These provisional and real sages may also temporarily dwell among the various devas of the triple world as retribution bodies.
Or, because he manifests in the human world, this land is called "the Abode of Commoners and Sages.

As for those called "sages," they refer to the various holy ones who have transcended the birth-and-death of the triple realm through the four fruits of the śrāvaka and above. As for those called "commoners," [they refer to ordinary beings].

This refers to all sentient beings within the six realms and three paths, from the heavens and humans downward, who have not yet transcended the birth-and-death of the triple world through segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

Because the mind possesses both delusion and awakening, there is the distinction between the holy and the ordinary. Once this distinction between the holy and the ordinary is established, there consequently arise the four lands and the ten realms.
Although the four lands are vast and boundless, they are ultimately nothing more than what is invoked by this single mind alone. As it is said:
There would be no such thing as death with a physical body, nor any distinction between the internal and external realms.

Furthermore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would have no occasion to employ their compassionate vows, nor any occasion to perform acts of transformation and deliverance. This is the general outline of the dimensions of this world, the true meaning of the triple realm (*tridhātu*).
Within each heaven and earth, each sun and moon, and each Mount Sumeru—from the first dhyāna heaven above...
From the Brahma-heaven below up to the realm of the Yama-rāja hell at the Iron Encircling Mountains above constitutes a single small world-system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
A thousand such small world-systems are covered by one Heaven of the Second Dhyāna; this is a single small thousandfold world-system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
When these small thousandfold world-systems are accumulated to the number of one thousand, they are covered by one Heaven of the Third Dhyāna. This is...
A single medium chiliocosm consists of one million small worlds. When these medium chiliocosms accumulate to one thousand, there is a Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna that covers them;
this is a great trichiliocosm, which consists of ten million times one hundred thousand small worlds.
One great trichiliocosm constitutes the entire sphere of transformation and salvation for a single Buddha, and is also termed the "three thousand [small worlds]."
"Great Trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) is a term used to express vastness and complexity without weariness. "Transformation and deliverance" (*huàdù*) refers to transformation;

it denotes the deliverance of those sentient beings within the realms of the three worlds and six paths who are subject to the cycle of birth and death (*bhavacakra*). Among those transformed and delivered by the Buddha, from the Bodhisattvas downward, all are embraced and included without exception;
yet, among them, those sentient beings within the realms subject to the cycle of birth and death are considered the most urgent priority. This must not be overlooked.
It is known. The realm converted and delivered by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the former Buddha, is called the Sahā world.
That which we inhabit is but one small world within this Sahā world. This small world consists of four great continents;
that governed by the Middle Kingdom is the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa), so named because it lies to the south of Mount Sumeru. It is also called...
China is also called Zhendan; this refers to what the *Loutan jing* (Kāṣyapaparivarta-sūtra) calls "Zhendan, east of the Onion River.
Since the void of the eight directions and above and below is inexhaustible, worlds are inexhaustible. Since worlds are inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible.
Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, birth and death are inexhaustible. Since birth and death are inexhaustible, the work of transformation and deliverance is inexhaustible.
Thus, the Buddhas themselves are also inexhaustible, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there are both pure and defiled lands. This Sahā world is currently a defiled land because the evil karma of its sentient beings perceives other regions as even more so;
therefore, it alone manifests as this defiled land. Although pure lands in other directions are numerous, [this one is distinct].
Only the Western World of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha unifies the four lands into a single land.

It eternally severs the sufferings of the three miserable paths, the six realms of existence, and the birth-and-death of segmented existence; therefore, it alone is purely pure, surpassing all other pure lands in the ten directions.
Its transformative teachings, its causes and effects, and all its adornments of the environment and its inhabitants are exactly as described in the original sutra.

Upon detailed examination, it is evident that the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies to the west of this Sahā world, at a distance of ten trillion Buddha-worlds from here; this is exactly as described in the original sutra.

Nowadays, the Chan school and various secular scholars fail to consult the Tripitaka, instead asserting that it corresponds to India in the Western Regions. This is a profound error. Furthermore, this...
This is a general overview of the worlds of the ten directions and the location of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
As for what is called the "scope of the mind" (*citta-mātra*): since space is inexhaustible and worlds are inexhaustible, the scope of the minds of sentient beings is likewise inexhaustible.
The "scope of the mind" refers to the extent that the mind can reach. For all Buddhas, this scope encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.

Having already penetrated the phenomena and principles of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and currently treading upon its sublime state, this constitutes the "mind-measure of one who has already realized" (*sākṣātkṛta-cittamātra*).
As for sentient beings who still linger within birth and death, although they cannot yet suddenly tread upon that state, it is not that they cannot first penetrate its phenomena and principles;
by means of this, they may gradually reach that sublime state. This constitutes the "mind-measure of one who has not yet realized. [The mind-measure] of one who has already realized...
The measure of the mind is inconceivable; even the measure of the mind before realization is inconceivable.

This is precisely what the ancient sages meant when they said that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in the three respects. Now, the distance between a Buddha and a sentient being cannot be measured by days or kalpas;
why then do we now consider them to be without distinction? It is because if one truly wishes to take the mind of a sentient being as...
If one is good, one will ultimately reach goodness. If one intends to do evil, one will ultimately reach evil. If one truly desires to study the Way, there is no way one will not study the Way.

If one truly desires to recite the Buddha’s name, there is no way one will not recite the Buddha’s name. If one truly desires to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], there is likewise no way one will not attain rebirth.

Whether one delights in worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one remains within worldly truth; or whether one delights in the world-transcending (lokottara), there is nothing that does not transcend the world.
From the Buddhas above down to the hells below, there is nothing that is not created by this single mind alone. This is what was revealed by the Buddhas of the past.
Having already caused the entire trichiliocosm to tremble, sentient beings below remain entirely without understanding, thinking that this has nothing to do with them.
I do not know for certain whether it truly has nothing to do with them; I simply dare not be so presumptuous.
Is this not why the Buddhas of the ten directions grieve and reflect upon them without ceasing? Therefore, [it is said]: "The Pure Land is only the pure mind."
That which is the self-nature of Amitābha is none other than the mind-nature of these sentient beings; it is merely that their minds perceive a defiled land.
That which is the self-nature of the three miserable realms is likewise none other than the mind-nature of these sentient beings; it depends solely upon the sentient beings' own choices.
Master Hongli said: "The single thought-moment of our present consciousness is entirely true and yet becomes deluded; entirely deluded and yet is precisely true.

Throughout the day it remains unchanging, yet throughout the day it follows conditions. If one does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm while reciting the Buddha’s name, one will instead recite for the nine realms.

If one does not recite for the Three Vehicles, one will instead recite for the six mundane realms. If one does not recite for the human and heavenly realms, one will instead recite for the three [evil paths]."

On the path, one does not think of ghosts or animals, but rather thinks of the hells. Since all who possess a mind cannot be without thought, the essence of the mind that is free from thought is realized by the Buddha alone.
From the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward, all possess thought; whenever a single thought arises, [it is so].
One will inevitably fall within the ten realms; there is no thought that can transcend these ten realms, for there is nothing outside the ten dharma-realms.
Every single thought that arises serves as a condition for a future birth. If one understands this principle and yet does not practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, [one is lost].

Such a thing has never occurred. If this mind can correspond with the merit of the Dharma-realm and the physical realm (the *niśraya* and *pratishthā*) through equal great kindness and great compassion, as well as with the vast names of the myriad virtues, it is precisely the mindfulness of the Buddha-dharmadhātu.

If it can correspond with the bodhicitta, the six perfections, and the myriad practices, it is precisely the mindfulness of the Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu. By means of the mind of non-self, [one corresponds] with the twelve links of dependent origination...
To be associated with this is to contemplate the dharma-realm of the pratyekabuddhas. To observe the Four Truths with a mind free of self is to contemplate the dharma-realm of the śrāvakas.
To be associated with the four dhyānas, the eight samādhis, and the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions is to contemplate the dharma-realm of the devas.
To be associated with the five precepts is to contemplate the dharma-realm of humans. If one cultivates the goodness of the precepts...
If one harbors thoughts of anger, pride, and competitiveness toward these dharmas, one immediately falls into the dharma-realm of the asuras.
If one applies lax and gentle mindfulness to the lower grade of the ten evil deeds, one falls into the dharma-realm of animals.

If one applies a mind that is half-lax and half-urgent in conjunction with the middle grade of the ten evil deeds, one then falls into the dharma-realm of hungry ghosts. If one applies a fierce and blazing mind to the upper grade of the ten...
If one corresponds with evil, one immediately falls into the dharma-realm of hell. The ten evils are:
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, harsh speech, double-tongued speech, greed, anger, and wrong views. To act contrary to these constitutes the ten virtues.
One should secretly examine for oneself which realm one’s daily arising thoughts correspond to most frequently, and with which realm they correspond.
This is what is meant by being "fierce. Then, on another day, as for the place where one establishes one's body and sustains one's life, there will be no need to trouble oneself by asking others.

It is further said: "All realms of experience are solely evoked by karma and solely manifested by the mind. At the very moment they manifest, their substance is identical to the mind. For all that possesses mind, it is impossible not to have objects.
If the realm of the Buddhas does not manifest, then the realms of the nine divisions manifest; if these do not manifest, then [the realms of] the three [evil paths manifest]."

When the realm of the [six] vehicles is manifested, the realms of the six classes of ordinary beings appear; when those realms of devas, humans, ghosts, and animals do not appear, then the realm of hell appears.
Although the realms manifested by the Buddhas and those of the Three Vehicles differ in their degree of excellence, they all essentially consist of the enjoyment of the bliss of the Dharma.
As for the realms manifested by the various devas of the triple world, they consist solely of the enjoyment of the bliss of meditative concentration and the five desires.
In the realm of human beings, suffering and pleasure alternate, each according to the varying degrees of one’s karma.
In the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, suffering predominates while pleasure is scarce. As for the hells, there is nothing but extreme suffering.

Just as the mountains, rivers, people, and objects manifested in a person’s dream all appear based on the dreaming mind—if there were no dreaming mind, there would certainly be no dreamscapes; even if the dreaming [mind] were absent...
There is no objective realm, nor is there a dreaming mind; therefore, one knows that outside the mind there is no realm, and outside the realm there is no mind.

The entire realm is the mind, and the entire mind is the realm. If one examines the effect within the cause, one must contemplate the mind; if one tests the cause at the place of the effect, one must contemplate the realm.
Thus it is said: there has never been a mind without a realm, nor a realm without a mind. The effect must follow from the cause; as for the cause...

It must surely be so. If one truly understands the principle that this mind and its objects, cause and effect, are of one suchness and non-dual, yet still refuses to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, I do not believe it possible.
The meaning of the "measure of the mind" (*citta-pramāṇa*) and the "measure of the world" (*loka-pramāṇa*) is fully set forth in the Tripitaka scriptures;
they are too numerous to cite in full. What the Great Master has discussed here alone is able to grasp the essential framework and the guiding principles, without the slightest error.
Regarding the remaining aggregates (*skandhas*), the student may also gain a general understanding from this.

In my impartial assessment, during the fifty years that the Buddha first preached the Dharma, he tirelessly instructed the holy and the ordinary across the nine realms; it was as if he had spent his entire life doing so in a single day.
One grows weary [of saṃsāra] until finally reaching nirvāṇa. Why do we not say "expounding the teachings" or "discussing the Way," but rather simply "preaching the Dharma"?
It is because that which was revealed by the Buddhas of the past is none other than the actual Dharma for liberation from birth and death.
The ways in which sentient beings create karma are myriad and diverse, encompassing every possible variation; therefore, the Buddhas of the past saved sentient beings.
The methods of the Dharma are also ten thousandfold and myriad in their differences, encompassing everything without exception. Now, summarizing the major outlines, there are generally five schools:

namely, the Chan School, the Pure Land School, the Teaching School, the Vinaya School, and the Esoteric School. Within the Chan School, there are five: known as the Guiyang, [Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan].
They are Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. The Pure Land school is singular; Mount Lu is its locus.
The doctrinal schools are threefold: Tiantai, Xianshou, and Cien. Tiantai and Xianshou constitute the School of Nature (Xingzong), while Cien constitutes the School of Characteristics (Xiangzong).
The Vinaya school is singular; Nanshan is its locus. Although the Esoteric school has no [specific lineage...]

[This lineage] was not included [in the official records], and thus its ancestral origins were not clearly manifest. Its founding patriarch was the National Teacher Vajrabodhi of Guangfu Temple in Luoyang.
In the Chan school, the ultimate goal is the direct realization of one's original nature, and the method of practice is the investigation of the *huatou* (critical phrase).
In the Pure Land school, the ultimate goal is rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and the method of practice is single-minded recitation.
The Amitābha Buddha is the method for practice. The doctrines and principles of the Teaching School (Jiaozong) are manifold;

its study comprises both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), all of which take the severing of delusions and the realization of the fruit as their ultimate goal. The various schools' methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* serve as the methods of practice.

However, the severing of delusions and the realization of the fruit are common to all schools; it is not unique to the Teaching School alone. Nevertheless, what the Teaching School discusses is especially detailed and thorough.

Regarding the dharmas of the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*): there is the meditation of the six subtle gates; there are the sixteen stages of special excellence (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*); there is the contemplation of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vipaśyanā*); there is the contemplation of the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā-vipaśyanā*);

there is the contemplation of the eight recollections (*aṣṭasmṛti-vipaśyanā*); there is the contemplation of the ten notions (*daśasaṃjñā-vipaśyanā*); there is the contemplation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa-vipaśyanā*); and there is the contemplation of the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana-vipaśyanā*).
There are the ten universal bases (daśa-kṛtsnāyatana). There are the nine successive concentrations (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti). There is the lion’s bound (siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi).

There is the transcendent concentration (vyutkrāntaka-samādhi). There is the king concentration (rāja-samādhi). One studies all dharmas with wisdom. There is the arousal of the mind of a śrāvaka. There is the arousal of the mind of a pratyekabuddha.

There is the arousal of the mind of the four great vows and the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). There is the contemplation of the essence of emptiness (svabhāva-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā). There is the threefold contemplation in succession. There is the perfect [contemplation].

The sudden and wondrous contemplation. Thus, the cultivation of concentration is called *śamatha* (stopping), and the cultivation of wisdom is called *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). The three contemplations are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
This sudden and wondrous contemplation of the Perfect Teaching is also termed the "Three Contemplations in One Mind" (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*) and is also known as the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
It is also titled *The Dharma-Gate of Mahāyāna Śamatha and Vipaśyanā*. The aforementioned śamathas and vipaśyanās encompass all the various vehicles, both Great and Small;
they are all studies for transcending the world. Beyond these, there are further the four fundamental dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

There are four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), all of which are meditative concentrations belonging to the realm of form. Generally speaking, there are four types of meditative concentration:
first, mundane meditation (*laukika-dhyāna*), which consists of the four fundamental dhyānas, as well as the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*) and the four formless absorptions.
As for those who practice it, they only realize celestial fruits and cannot transcend birth-and-death within the limits of temporal segmentation; therefore, it is called "worldly.
Second is meditation that is both worldly and world-transcending, namely the Six Sublime Gates, the Sixteen Special Victories, and the Contemplation of Penetrating Clarity.

Those of sharp faculties rely on these to give rise to true realization and sever delusions, while those of dull faculties may also take rebirth according to their meditative states; therefore, it is called "also."
The world and the supramundane are both encompassed by the single contemplation of the essence of emptiness within the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*), which likewise governs the Three Vehicles.
Only the sequential threefold contemplation and the wondrous contemplation of the Perfect-Sudden (*yuan-dun*) are exclusively the methods for the practice of the Mahāyāna.

Nevertheless, although the names of these various systems of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* remain extant, those who actually cultivate them are few. Among those in recent times whose aspirations are set upon the supramundane, for the most part, or...

One may return to the Chan school, or return to the Pure Land school; yet whether it be Chan, Teaching, or Vinaya, one should especially regard the dedication of merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land as the primary principle.

This is because the various schools are complex and many lead to regression and decline, whereas the method of "horizontal transcendence" over birth and death achieves twice the result with half the effort.
Should one realize the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, it is particularly sufficient to encompass all other schools; indeed, this very samādhi...

This has not yet been achieved; however, if one can maintain right mindfulness at the moment of death, one may still attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Once rebirth is attained, there will forever be no cause for falling back.
Thus, the difference between these outcomes is as vast as that between heaven and abyss, and it is something that cannot be equated with other schools.
The Vinaya school regards the simultaneous purification of body and mind as its ultimate goal, maintaining the full set of precepts from the bodhisattva level downward.
This is the method for practice and maintenance. Having already received the precepts, if one subsequently violates them, the offense may reach a point where repentance is no longer possible.
In recent times, those who receive the precepts treat the violation of them as a "samādhi of playful sport.

One need not inquire further to know their fate regarding the merits and demerits that lead to either elevation or downfall. The Esoteric School consists of the recitation of various *dhāraṇī* mantras. As for *dhāraṇī*:
This is called "total retention" (*dhāraṇī*), for it can encompass all Buddha-dharmas. What is meant by total retention? It refers to those who maintain and recite *dhāraṇīs*;
they not only repent of past karma, but also purify their mental karma, deliver sentient beings, and eliminate calamities and hardships.
It can also subdue ghosts and spirits; it can redirect one’s rebirth toward the Pure Land; and it can sever all delusions, clarifying the fundamental mind and realizing one’s own true nature.
However, the practitioner must maintain the precepts, observe silence, remain in seclusion, and focus their recitation with single-minded devotion.

Only when the recitation reaches the state of "one mind undisturbed" can one realize samādhi in this very life and achieve all that is sought according to one’s wishes. This is not as in ordinary practice.

If one’s mindfulness is scattered, its efficacy will likewise diminish; it cannot be generalized. The various sūtras of the Tripiṭaka constitute the Exoteric section, while the various dhāraṇīs constitute the Esoteric section.
What is called "Exoteric" means interpreting the meaning according to the text and initiating practice based on that interpretation; there is nothing therein that cannot be understood.
What is called "Esoteric" means transcribing the sounds without translating the meaning, like the oral passwords or signal arrows used within an army.
It is only fitting that this be delivered so that it may be practiced and upheld. One should respond without error; there is no need to seek an interpretation, nor is it necessary to seek one at all.
Therefore, those who maintain the recitation should simply chant according to the text; there is no other method.

Yet the ignorant do not understand this, and instead harbor doubts because they cannot comprehend the meaning. Furthermore, there are certain reckless monastics who, unaware of this principle, insist on providing forced interpretations.
Commentary: This is indeed strange. Food is for the purpose of curing hunger; yet one suddenly demands that it also ward off the cold. Clothing is for the purpose of warding off the cold;
yet one suddenly demands that it also cure hunger. Not knowing where their respective functions lie, such claims are all erroneous and deluded speech.
These various *dhāraṇīs*—some issued from the Buddha’s own teaching, some from the teaching of *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas, and some from spirits—[are likewise misunderstood].

The deity said: "As for those whose majestic spiritual power is brilliant and whose divine efficacy is unfathomable, there are the Great Compassionate One (Mahākāruṇika), Uṣṇīṣavijayā, Cundā, Śūraṅgama, and other such dhāraṇīs.
Each of these dhāraṇīs has its own root sūtra, and the methods for their recitation and ritual protocols are numerous.

However, to observe the precepts, maintain silence, seclude oneself within a closed door, and focus one's mind exclusively on the practice is the primary principle. As for the rest, there is no need to be overly constrained or attached."
The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of Great Compassion Endowed with Vision* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* state this; yet common people do not understand these teachings.

Some, bound by the literal text and drawn by their own interpretations, dare not even recite them. Others, being deluded, treat them with arbitrary contempt, thereby incurring the reproach and condemnation of ghosts and spirits.
These are all the faults of the ignorant and base, and are not worth discussing. As for the four characters of "A-mi-tuo-fo" (Amitābha Buddha), they are all...

These belong to the Sanskrit tradition and are likewise identical to various mantras. Therefore, the methods for reciting mantras and recollecting the Buddha (*nien-fo*) are, for the most part, no different.
The ultimate goal of recollecting the Buddha lies solely in rebirth in the Pure Land, with practices such as repentance and vows being subsumed as secondary aspects.

In contrast, the practice of reciting mantras focuses primarily on repentance and vows, with rebirth in the Pure Land being subsumed as a secondary aspect. These are the various methods of cultivation within these five schools. All...
This is what students ought to know.

What the Buddhas of the past called the "complete embodiment" consists of no more than two aspects: first, True Suchness (*tathatā*); second, Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). It is precisely this.
To clarify one's own fundamental mind and perceive one's own original nature, thereby subduing and eliminating the three delusions—this is True Suchness (*tathatā*).

To have not yet clarified the fundamental mind and not yet perceived the original nature, with the three delusions fully present—this is birth-and-death (*saṃskṛta*). True Suchness is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing;
it is that which is equally possessed by the four classes of noble beings who transcend the world and the six categories of ordinary beings within the triple world.
This is the fundamental nature. As for arising and ceasing: it both arises and ceases; it is both defiled and pure; it both increases and decreases.
From the three realms and six classes of ordinary beings up to the Bodhisattvas of the *sambhoga-kāya* adorned with the true recompense, these are the three delusions that they all possess in common.

The three delusions are: first, the delusion of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); second, the delusion of *rajas* (dust-like ignorance); and third, the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the delusion of views and thoughts: it belongs to the sentient beings of the three realms.

Delusion (*moha*). The delusions of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* are as numerous as motes of dust in a sunbeam. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the delusion of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Sentient beings within the three realms encompass these three types of delusion, possessing them all without exception; yet, among them, the single delusion of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) is especially regarded as the root of birth-and-death through segmented transformation (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*).
For this reason, the teachings establish the Three Contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) to shatter the three delusions and realize the [Three Truths].

Wisdom accomplishes the three virtues. Those who cultivate the contemplation of emptiness destroy the afflictions of views and thoughts, realize all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), and accomplish the virtue of prajñā.

Those who cultivate the contemplation of the conventional destroy the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust, realize the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgākārajñatā*), and accomplish the virtue of liberation. Those who cultivate the contemplation of the middle...
They shatter the delusions of ignorance and realize the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby perfecting the virtues of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Having already shattered the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), they are subsequently able to ascend through and realize the four fruits of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas. They transcend the cycle of birth and death characterized by fragmentation (*pariccheda-utpāda-maraṇa*), which is what is meant by "transcending the world.

Furthermore, by shattering the delusions of the sands of the Ganges and partially breaking through the ignorance of the fundamental nature, they are then able to realize the stages of a Bodhisattva up to the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*).

All fruits [of practice] further exhaustively shatter ignorance; once the three delusions are completely shattered, one immediately realizes the fruit of Buddhahood, which is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
As the three delusions are shattered sequentially, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is progressively revealed.

Only when the three delusions are exhausted and shattered without remainder does True Suchness become fully endowed with all qualities; this is precisely the essence and function of the Buddhas of the past.
There is nothing that is not fully provided therein; such is the teaching of this school.

As for the method of investigating through *dhyāna*, one must apply the mind with sharp acuity and polish it until reaching the subtlest degree, necessarily breaking through the final, sturdy barrier before it can be called "thorough awakening.

Once one has reached thorough awakening, the three delusions are all severed, and one’s sole task is to purify the currently active *pravṛtti-vijñānas*. This is because [it is achieved] through wisdom.

Because he entered into meditative concentration (*samādhi*), his realization was seen to be so transcendent and eminent. This is the same as that realized by the Sixth Patriarch Dajian of the Middle Kingdom and the various masters of the Five Houses.
However, in later generations, the karmic force of sentient beings has become increasingly thick while their power of the Way has become increasingly feeble;
thus, within the school of Chan, even slight deviations in what is awakened to or cultivated lead to many sighs of lamentation over being at a fork in the road. Above.
Since those of superior faculties are but one in ten thousand, even if one has attained a slight awakening, it is utterly insufficient to rely upon for the sudden transcendence of birth and death.
Consequently, it cannot compare with the Pure Land school, which effectively benefits practitioners of all three capacities. Master Yongming Yanshou said:
"Those who have Chan but no Pure Land—nine out of ten will go astray. When the realm of the intermediate state suddenly appears before them, they are startled in an instant."
Let him go as he will. The words spoken by those of mature realization are as clear and evident as this. Those who truly aspire to liberation from birth and death must not fail to understand them.
The various schools that cultivate *dhyāna* seek liberation as a means to emerge vertically from birth and death;
the single school of Pure Land cultivation seeks liberation as a means to emerge horizontally from birth and death. "Emerging vertically" refers to ascending from below;

it means attaining liberation by severing delusions and realizing the fruits of enlightenment solely within this realm. "Emerging horizontally" refers to moving from here to there; it means being reborn in the Western [Pure Land].
The Pure Land is for the purpose of transcending birth and death. Transcending birth and death vertically relies solely on one’s own power;

as long as even a hair’s breadth of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) remains unsevered, one cannot achieve liberation from all burdens. Transcending birth and death horizontally relies both upon one’s own power and the power of the Buddha;

even if the afflictions of views and thought are not yet severed, one can still attain rebirth there. Once rebirth is attained, no further karma can be created, and there will forever be no falling back into decline.

Regarding "preparation" (*yu*): it is as clarified in the original sutra. Although one has not yet severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-āsrava*), which is not the ultimate state for rebirth, if at the time of death one’s right mindfulness is clear and one does not cease reciting the Buddha’s name, rebirth can be considered certain.

When compared with the various other schools that teach vertical emergence, there is indeed a distinction between difficulty and ease. This is because our Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, and those of the ten directions...
This is why all the Buddhas have praised it in unison; this is also why the masters of the various schools from the Tang and Song dynasties onward have exhorted others with all their might.
The discussions of our predecessors are already extremely detailed, and even this very sutra reveals that there is no need for weariness [with its message];
thus, further elaboration would be superfluous. If you can truly seek out the underlying reason for this, do not treat the orthodox teaching of liberation as a mere tool for empty talk.
This is sufficient.

My central argument is that one should single-mindedly cultivate pure karma in order to aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; this constitutes the Pure Land School (Jingzong). As for the branches of the Pure Land School:
There are several other schools of thought. First is the recitation of the name; second is the visualization and contemplation;

third is the recitation of Mahāyāna dhāraṇī mantras with the dedication of merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land; fourth is the recitation of various Mahāyāna sūtras with the dedication of merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land.
These teachings are fully presented in the various sūtras and cannot be recounted exhaustively here; yet, in the end, the recitation of the name is considered the foremost practice.
To uphold the True Dharma and to uphold the Name means to recite "Amitābha Buddha" with the mouth and contemplate it with the mind; this is what is meant.

The method for visualization is detailed in the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*. Although this is also a major pillar of pure karma, the visualized realm is vast and expansive.

This is beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings. Furthermore, there is the need to guard against both correct and erroneous contemplation; its complexities and difficulties are truly extreme.
Consequently, from ancient times to the present, there has never been anyone who exclusively practiced visualization to seek rebirth in the Pure Land—the difficulty of which can thus be understood.
Moreover, the essence of visualization lies solely in seeing the Buddha face-to-face, yet this requires the fruit of recitation to reach the state of single-mindedness.

Even in times of chaos, one will inevitably behold the Buddha face-to-face; furthermore, the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants in the Land of Ultimate Bliss will all appear before one’s eyes.
As described in ancient scriptures such as the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and as realized by the late Master Xingyun, all these things are indeed present.
This single school of holding the name is sufficient to encompass both visualization and contemplation; there is no need to seek anything else.

It is easier to abandon what is simple than to pursue what is difficult. This is why practitioners of the Pure Land path throughout both ancient and modern times have invariably taken this sutra as the primary practice for rebirth.
Although there are explanations regarding various other gates of practice, such as the recitation of mantras, those who actually cultivate them are few.

For liberation from birth and death is the foremost and most significant undertaking for human beings; were one to understand its significance, they would certainly never be content to set aside the primary practice for the sake of expediency.
They instead rush toward peripheral paths in hopes of seeking some fortunate outcome.

Those who practice the path of purity must first possess the two wheels of faith and aspiration; it should be understood that if these two wheels are lacking, one will certainly be unable to give rise to practice based on understanding.
As for the precursors to these two wheels, there are two matters: the first is the thorough investigation of the scriptures.
First, one must rely on teachers and seek out friends. Without the classics, teachers and friends would have no means to exercise the function of admonition and exhortation;
without teachers and friends, the classics would have no way to achieve the effect of inspiring observation and emulation.
Indeed, teachers and friends are the living classics, and the classics are the refined teachers and friends. Neither may be neglected. Thus, liberation arises.
The ultimate Way of death is not something that can be grasped by those who are negligent, deluded, or perverse.

Once these two matters are completed and the two wheels are fully prepared, one can then rely on understanding to give rise to practice and cultivate it without doubt; such are the heroes who transcend the world.
If one’s mother were to follow the path of the narrow and the simple, she might instead suffer a sudden fall from which she could never recover.

Regarding the central teaching on the four methods of chanting the Buddha’s name, there are likewise two approaches: first, chanting the four-character name of the Buddha; second, chanting the six-character name of the Buddha. As for chanting the six characters...

Reciting the four-character name of the Buddha refers to the sixteenth visualization (*guan*) of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, which states: "With palms joined and hands crossed, recite 'Namo Amitābha Buddha'.
This is it. Reciting the four characters of the Buddha's name is found in both the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (the "Root Sūtra") and the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*. As the Root Sūtra says:
"Exclusively and single-mindedly mindful of Amitābha Buddha," and "There remains only the four characters 'Amitābha Buddha,' by which all are extensively delivered."
This refers to all sentient beings. Furthermore, it is as stated in the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* regarding "grasping and upholding the name.

Although the four characters and the six characters appear to be no different, it is specifically the recitation of the four characters that originates from this very sūtra; moreover, the two characters "Namo" ultimately belong to supplementary text.
Therefore, those who practice the path of Pure Land should especially take the single-minded recitation of the four-character Buddha-name as their primary practice.

This is the correct path. There are three matters for cultivating the practice of purity: first, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, upholding the precepts; and third, cultivating merit. Mindfulness of the Buddha is the primary practice (*maula-pratipatti*);
upholding the precepts and cultivating merit are the auxiliary practices (*sahakāri-pratipatti*). This is what is meant by "arising from understanding into practice."
The method of Buddha-recitation (nienfo) further consists of three categories: first, the regular fixed recitation; second, the regular informal recitation;

and third, the intensive recitation within a closed retreat for a set period to realize the samādhi of direct manifestation. The specific method of intensive recitation will be seen in the subsequent text.

The two sessions of concentrated and dispersed practice constitute the orthodox path for the cultivation of pure karma; therefore, I shall first set forth their exposition as an instruction for beginners.
In these remote and uncultivated regions, people do not even know what the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) entails, so I do not regret being prolix.

Regarding the fixed daily practice of Buddha-recitation: one should first prepare a clean room and offer a golden image of the Three Sages of the Western Paradise, or a single hanging scroll of their images.
The images must face east, and the practitioner must face west when performing prostrations; only then is it said to accord with the ritual protocol. At the time of the daily recitation:
First, wash your hands and rinse your mouth, and burn incense. Then, join your palms and face west, prostrating with a sincere heart and paying homage by touching the ground with your head.
Having completed the prostrations, recite: "Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. Next, say:
Homage to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Next, say:
Homage to Amitābha Buddha, the Teacher who Welcomes and Guides in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. Next, say:
Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Next, say: Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Next, say:
Homage to the Assembly of Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean. Having finished the prostrations and recitation, one should then recite the [Verses of] Master Zuo... of Yunqi.
It is equally appropriate to recite the "Vow Text for the Western Land" once, or to recite the "Verse of Dedication and Aspiration of the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion" once.
Although these texts differ in their brevity and detail, their essential meaning is no different;
for both primarily focus on dedication toward rebirth in the Pure Land, and both comprehensively encompass the four great vows of the Bodhisattvas without omission. Dedication...
Having finished [the recitation], one then withdraws and sits facing west.

With a sincere mind, one invokes the name of Amitābha Buddha—either a thousand times, several thousand times, or up to ten thousand times, as the case may be. Having completed the recitation, one again prostrates and withdraws.
This is the ritual procedure for the fixed daily practice. [This concludes] the section on the Pure Great Ocean Assembly of Bodhisattvas and above.
To establish a sequence for the daily recitation: the invocation and mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha constitutes the primary practice.

Regarding the fixed daily recitation, the specific times, as well as the number of recitations, are all to be determined by the practitioner themselves according to their own circumstances and capacity;
there is no fixed schedule. For instance, if one is traveling abroad and unable to provide offerings or perform prostrations before an image, one should simply join the palms while facing west.
Establishing the ritual, one must contemplate Amitābha Buddha and recite verses for the dedication of merit; these, too, must not be omitted.

Regarding what is called "informal practice" (*sanke*): apart from one's daily fixed practice, at any time and in any place—provided one is free from affairs and not in the presence of guests—one should, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, invoke the name of Amitābha Buddha, either silently holding it in mind or [reciting it aloud].
Regarding the method of recitation, one may either recite aloud or perform *vajra-japa*; both are acceptable. However, it is not necessary to use a rosary to keep count.
As for *vajra-japa*, this refers to moving the lips and teeth slightly so that each syllable is distinct and clear, yet no sound is produced.

The aforementioned ritual for fixed daily recitation varies between elaborate and concise according to ancient traditions; this [method] represents a balanced compromise and is therefore appropriate. It may be adopted as the standard.
This is a fixed rule. However, this refers specifically to the two groups of lay practitioners.

As for the two groups of monastics, they should ascend to the hall three times each day to perform prostrations and recitations; or, following the example of Mount Lu, they should practice the six-period liturgy.

Yet, these practices have long been neglected in the monasteries throughout the land, with some instead relying on their own sectarian establishments to gloss over their errors and distort the ancient traditions.
The Buddha’s sublime Dharma and noble intentions have become obscured and are no longer transmitted; this is truly a matter for deep lamentation.

Now, only those at Hongli Mountain maintain their practice with such rigorous discipline that, within just two or three years, there are those who attain rebirth through right mindfulness. This is truly worthy of respect.
As for the method of cultivating scattered mindfulness, both laypeople and monastics alike should practice it according to the Dharma; only then will it be effective.

One gradually reaps the fruits of single-minded concentration. If one cannot maintain mindfulness with every thought and action, rebirth in the Pure Land is truly not something one can venture to guarantee;

practitioners should reflect upon this themselves. As for the method of rebirth through ten recitations, although it originates from the sutra itself, according to my observations of various practitioners of pure karma, some may have cultivated their practice quite diligently, yet as they reach old age, they instead retreat from their initial resolve. Or, when facing...
At the time of death, there are those who occasionally experience a state of mental confusion and delusion such that they immediately lose right mindfulness;

yet, as for those who can achieve rebirth in the Pure Land simply by practicing the ten recitations, I have truly never personally witnessed such a case. This is because, in this age of the Dharma’s decline, the karmic habits of sentient beings grow increasingly thick.

Furthermore, these cannot be compared to the roots of goodness from three thousand years ago. Since I have not personally witnessed it, I do not dare rely on the text to claim realization for myself, lest I mislead both myself and others.
Let those of broad learning examine this. The *Vow for Rebirth in the Western Land* by Yunqi says:
"I bow my head to the Land of Peace and Bliss in the West, to the Great Teacher who receives and guides sentient beings. I now make this vow."

I vow to be reborn there. May you, out of your compassion, graciously accept me. This disciple, [Name], on behalf of the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*, seeks the supreme path of the One Vehicle *bodhi* of all Buddhas above.

Therefore, with single-minded devotion, I hold fast to and recite the sublime name of Amitābha Buddha, endowed with myriad virtues, aspiring to be born in the Pure Land. Furthermore, because my karma is heavy and my merit is slight, and my hindrances are deep...

My wisdom is shallow; my defiled mind easily flares up, while pure virtue is difficult to achieve. Now, before the Buddha, I lift my five limbs in diligent devotion and pour out my single heart, offering sincere repentance.
From boundless kalpas until now, I and all sentient beings have been deluded regarding our inherently pure mind, indulging in greed, anger, and ignorance, thereby defiling the three karmas.
The immeasurable and boundless sinful stains we have committed, and the immeasurable and boundless fetters we have bound—[I now repent them all].
May all karmic debts of resentment be completely extinguished. From this day forth, I dare to establish profound vows: to distance myself from unwholesome dharmas and vow never to create them again;
to diligently cultivate the Noble Path and vow never to regress or fall away; to vow to attain Perfect Enlightenment; and to vow to deliver all sentient beings.
May Amitābha Buddha, by the power of his compassionate vows, bear witness to me, have pity on me, and bestow his grace upon me. May it be so!
Within the state of meditative contemplation or during the moments of sleep, may I behold the golden body of Amitābha Buddha;
may I traverse the jewel-adorned land of Amitābha Buddha; and may I receive the consecration of the nectar of immortality from Amitābha Buddha.
May his radiance illuminate my body, his hand stroke my head, and his robe cover my form, so that my past karmic obstructions are naturally eliminated and my roots of goodness increase.
Swiftly emptying afflictions and suddenly shattering ignorance, the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment is realized with vast clarity.
The true realm of tranquil light is constantly manifested before one. When the time of death arrives, one knows it beforehand;

the body is free from all illness, suffering, and calamity, and the mind is free from all attachment and delusion. The faculties are joyful and content, right mindfulness is clear and distinct, and one relinquishes the retribution-body.
Tranquil and composed, as if entering meditative absorption, Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of holy sages, emit light to welcome and guide us.

They lower their hands to lead us by the hand; towers, pavilions, banners, and streamers, along with extraordinary fragrances and celestial music, manifest the sacred realm of the West before our very eyes.
May all sentient beings who see or hear this feel joy and profound inspiration, and resolve to attain Bodhicitta. I...

At that time, riding upon a vajra-throne and following behind the Buddha, in the space of a finger-snap, they were born within a pool of the seven treasures in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, amidst a sublime lotus flower.
As the flower opened, they beheld the Buddha and saw all the bodhisattvas; they heard the wondrous sound of the Dharma and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
In an instant, they served the various Buddhas and personally received their prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Having received the prediction, [they... three...
Having fully accomplished the four bodies, the five wisdoms, the six supernormal powers, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharani-doors, and all merits,
they shall not depart from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), but will instead return to the Sahā world. There, manifesting countless emanations throughout the lands of the ten directions,
they shall deliver and liberate sentient beings through inconceivable and sovereign spiritual powers and various skillful means, causing them all to...
Free from defilement, may they regain their pure minds and be reborn together in the Western Land, entering the stage of non-retrogression.
Such great vows are inexhaustible as long as the world is inexhaustible, sentient beings are inexhaustible, and karma and afflictions are all inexhaustible; thus, my vows shall be inexhaustible.

May I now pay homage to the Buddha, make this aspiration, and cultivate meritorious virtue. May these merits be dedicated to all sentient beings, universally repaying the four debts of gratitude and providing sustenance for all within the three realms of existence.
May all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm together perfect the All-encompassing Wisdom. The verse for dedicating through Great Compassion and making vows says:
The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time—Amitābha is foremost among them. He delivers sentient beings in nine grades; his majestic power is infinite.
I now take great refuge and repent for the sins of my three karmas. Whatever merits and virtues I possess, I dedicate them with a sincere heart. May we all together recite the Buddha’s name.
For people, the response manifests according to the occasion; at the moment of death, the realm of the West appears clearly before one's eyes.

All who see and hear shall exert themselves with diligence and together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Having seen the Buddha, they will understand birth and death, and like the Buddha, they shall deliver all beings.
The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* states: "Those who cultivate the practice of purity shall be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three types of merit. First: filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, possessing a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten wholesome actions.
Second: receiving and upholding the Three Refuges, being fully endowed with the various precepts, and not violating dignified decorum."
Third is to resolve upon bodhicitta, to have deep faith in cause and effect, and to read and recite the Mahāyāna while encouraging other practitioners to do the same.
These three matters are called pure karma. The Buddha told Vaidehī: "Do you now know?
These three types of karma are the true causes for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Now, according to what the former Buddhas taught...

Regarding the various wholesome karmas that serve as the causal ground for manifesting the Pure Land, nothing is more detailed than this. It is sufficient to supplement what is lacking in the original sūtra.

Students should know that in this world of five turbidities, amidst the five pains and five burnings of all sufferings, one can never escape them unless one maintains these three pure karmas through diligent effort.
One should use mindfulness of the Buddha to rectify the inner mind and accumulate wholesome deeds to encourage outer conduct; only then—
One must become a member of the Pure Land school before one can attain rebirth in the Pure Land;

failing to do so, even if one practices mindfulness of the Buddha with diligence, it will merely run counter to the Bodhi of the Mahāyāna, as can be known from what is realized herein. These are the three pure karmas.
This is the actual practice of former Buddhas; you must not neglect seeking instruction therein.
As for why the first section does not speak of serving the sovereign with loyalty, it is because it addresses the two monastic orders who have left the household life.

For lay officials and gentlemen, being subjects and sons by nature, they should naturally act according to the precedents of filial support and service without waiting for further elaboration. This is the mind of compassion.
"Not killing" means not killing sentient beings. If one kills a person unjustly, it goes without saying that it is a transgression. Regarding the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*):
first, the three karmas of the body—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; second, the four karmas of speech—false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech;

third, the three karmas of the mind—covetousness, malice, and delusion. When these ten matters are practiced together, they are called the ten unwholesome karmas (*daśākuśala-karmapatha*). These ten matters...
These are all non-practiced; they are called the ten wholesome acts of restraint (*daśa saṃvara-kuśala*). Merely refraining from evil may also be called "wholesome.

Beyond these wholesome acts of restraint, if one is further able to turn back the ten evils and cultivate wholesome practices even more extensively, only then are they called the ten wholesome karmas (*daśa kuśala-karma*).

As for turning away from evil and cultivating goodness: beyond merely abstaining from killing, one is further able to ransom and release living beings and exercise caution and compassion regarding punishments. Not...

To refrain from arbitrarily sentencing a single person constitutes the wholesome karma of non-killing. Beyond refraining from theft, to further be able to provide relief to the poor and destitute constitutes the wholesome karma of non-stealing.
Beyond refraining from sexual misconduct, to further be able to preserve the integrity of chastity constitutes the wholesome karma of non-lust.
Beyond refraining from false speech, to further be able to employ discourse characterized by utmost sincerity and compassion...
To teach others to reform their faults and move toward goodness, and to resolve their doubts and study the Way, constitutes the wholesome karma of not speaking falsely.

Beyond the avoidance of frivolous speech, to be further able to use comprehensive and eloquent discourse to teach others to reform their faults and move toward goodness, and to resolve their doubts and study the Way, constitutes the wholesome karma of not engaging in frivolous speech. Beyond the avoidance of harsh speech, to furthermore be able to...

To teach others to reform their faults and move toward goodness, as well as to resolve their doubts and study the Way, by means of discourse that accords with human sentiment and measures the principles of reason, constitutes the wholesome karma of refraining from harsh speech (*pāruṣya-virati*).

Beyond refraining from divisive speech (*paiśunya-virati*), to further teach others to reform their faults and move toward goodness, as well as to resolve their doubts and study the Way, by means of discourse characterized by loyalty and sincerity, constitutes the wholesome karma of refraining from divisive speech. [Refraining from] greed...
Beyond this, he is further able to show affection for his kin and benevolence toward the people, extending from those near to those far away, bestowing gifts without weariness;

or he may recommend the worthy and yield to the capable, serving his sovereign through such human conduct and refusing to take office or emolument for selfish ends—this constitutes the wholesome karma of non-greed.
Beyond non-anger, he is further able to speak with bitter sincerity and maternal kindness to resolve the enmity between men and to settle their litigations and lawsuits—this constitutes non-anger.

Beyond the absence of delusion, being able to correctly establish righteousness and clarify the Way, and using virtue, wisdom, skill, and knowledge to maintain the governance and teachings of the state and the world, as well as during all times of peril, collapse, and disorder—this constitutes the wholesome karma of non-delusion;

it is the perfection of the ten wholesome paths of action. Regarding the meaning of these ten wholesome paths, each has three aspects: one negative, one positive, and one of restraint. Thus, there are three layers for each.
Regarding advancement and retreat, let us consider them in terms of the three realms. The ultimate fruit of supreme goodness is sufficient to lead one upward to birth among the various heavens;

the ultimate fruit of supreme evil is sufficient to cause one to sink downward into the Avīci Hell. Therefore, the established precept of the former Buddhas holds that only the ten wholesome actions constitute the direct cause for the heavenly path.
However, to fulfill their full measure, one must first cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, which will truly and eternally realize the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment].
This is the primary cause for Perfect Enlightenment. Therefore, in the causal stage of the Pure Land school, one must likewise take this as the essential core of meritorious karma.
According to the traditional explanation of the ten wholesome actions: beyond non-killing, there is only the release of living beings; beyond non-stealing, only the giving of food;
beyond non-lust, only the practice of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*); beyond non-lying, only sincerity; and beyond non-frivolous speech...
Beyond [the avoidance of] falsehood, there is only sincerity and straightforwardness; beyond [the avoidance of] double-tongued speech, there is only the reconciliation of disputes;
beyond [the avoidance of] harsh speech, there is only constant gentleness; beyond greed, there is only non-contention; beyond anger, there is only loving-kindness and compassion.

Apart from the absence of delusion, it is said that all things arise solely through causes and conditions; this is largely the doctrine of the lecturers. Therefore, [the previous discussion] spoke only from the perspective of those who have left the household life.
It was not realized that the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Paths established by the Buddha were intended to mold the fourfold assembly of both the ordained and the laity alike.
These principles are certainly not meant to be monopolized exclusively by the two groups of the ordained who are confined to a single corner of practice.

To practice stillness is merely to maintain oneself; to practice cultivation must lead to the transformation and liberation of sentient beings. This accords with the intent of the teachings established by the Buddhas of the past.
What is now spoken is not false, but only sincere and truthful; what is spoken is not ornate, but only plain and straightforward, and so forth.
Being confined to a single corner and failing to expand upon it, one truly cannot exhaust its full measure.

Now, this new exposition takes as its subject the essential duties of the fourfold assembly within the human realm, thereby expanding upon the meaning of the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) that remain unfulfilled. My own narrow and solitary views are not worth discussing further.
Regarding the "Three Refuges" (*triśaraṇa*): this refers to taking refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Regarding the "various precepts": this refers to...

There are the five precepts for laypeople; upon leaving the household life, one cultivates the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, the three hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣuṇī, as well as the bodhisattva’s ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.

Not violating the rules of deportment means that in all postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—one must not deviate even slightly from the monastic discipline. To generate the bodhi-mind...
"Upholding the mind" refers to the arousal of the four great vows of bodhicitta. The four great vows are: first, "Sentient beings are boundless;
I vow to deliver them all"; second, "Afflictions are inexhaustible; I vow to sever them all"; third, "Dharma gates are immeasurable;
I vow to study them all"; fourth, "The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; I vow to accomplish it. These four great vows constitute the ten [stages] of the Mahāyāna.
This is the direct cause for Bodhisattvas on the stages, and it is also the direct cause for the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions to realize the supreme fruit.
Although there are four types of vows, the vow to deliver sentient beings is the primary meaning. Only by making this vow does one become a follower of the Mahāyāna;

failing to make this vow constitutes the two lesser vehicles (Hīnayāna). While the fruits realized by these [lesser vehicles] are indeed transcendent beyond birth, [they do not lead to the ultimate liberation].
Beyond death, there will be no time when one ever attains Buddhahood; such a person is precisely what the Buddhas do not accept.

One must necessarily turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, and only then proceed directly toward Bodhi, advancing further and further upward. This is the distinction between the various vehicles, both Great and Small, and between those who attain Buddhahood and those who do not.
Those who practice the path of Pure Land should single-mindedly emulate Amitābha Buddha to make their vows.

Saving sentient beings is the primary objective. Even those who were unaware of making vows, once they have attained rebirth there, will inevitably turn from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.
This differs from those of the two vehicles in other worlds who remain ultimately confined to the partial teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.

Therefore, in the three grades of rebirth described in this sutra, it is invariably stated that one must "give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi. This applies to those who have deep faith in cause and effect.
The cause is spoken of in terms of "seeds," while the fruit is spoken of in terms of "fruits. It is like the cultivation of trees in a farm or garden:
one must first sow the seeds, and only then will the fruits be formed. In the world, there is no fruit without a seed, nor is there a seed without a fruit.

These two characters are the general names for the myriad principles and myriad affairs of the ten realms and four lands, both mundane and supramundane. Yet, the common folk have failed to investigate this, and thus [they] only...

To claim that the retribution of good and evil corresponds [to the cause] is erroneous. For although the response of good and evil is indeed contained within the framework of cause and effect, it is not the correct definition of the actual meaning of "cause" and "effect.

To treat the response of good and evil as the entirety of cause and effect is like insisting that a single piece of wood or a single stone constitutes a mountain, or that a single finger or a single joint constitutes a person; it is to mistake the mountain for the wood and the person for the finger.

He would certainly not consent to it. Those who read and recite the Mahāyāna—the various scriptures and teachings of the Mahāyāna—are the primary causes for transforming and delivering sentient beings and advancing toward the ultimate fruit;
they cannot be compared to the limited learning of the Hīnayāna, which seeks only self-benefit.

Therefore, those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land must take a thorough understanding of the Mahāyāna as the profound source of their path. To encourage practitioners [in this], [one must consider] birth and death...

For this reason, the method of liberation cannot be suddenly understood by ordinary beings of the mundane world; it must rely upon the exhortation and guidance of teachers and friends before one can realize and enter it.
This is especially the essential principle for delivering sentient beings. Therefore, exhortation is further established as the conclusion of the practice of purity.
The three blessings mentioned above are the auxiliary practices of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) and also the fundamental framework of all myriad virtues.
Regarding all wholesome karmas, mundane and supramundane, there is none that they do not govern; thus, the Buddhas of the past have also taken these as the primary cause for pure karma.

However, unless one recollects the Buddha with a sincere heart and directs merit toward rebirth [in the Pure Land], these three blessings will lack a guide from the outset and will merely result in the fruits of humans or devas. This, then, is the true meaning of "auxiliary practice. To treat this:
The sūtras must be examined with care.
The study of the Pure Land has six essentials; when these six essentials are fully mastered, one will attain radiant, great awakening and become a peer of the Buddhas.
That which is fully realized lies even beyond the various schools of Chan and the doctrinal teachings.
If the six essentials are not all understood, one will remain trapped in saṃsāra and fail to transcend birth and death; what end could there be? Even the Buddhas cannot foresee such an outcome.
What are these six essentials? They are precept, concentration, and wisdom—these are the three supramundane virtues. Those who cultivate the practice of purity rely upon them...

These three virtues each possess both provisional and ultimate aspects. Although the great masters of the Pure Land school in the past have not explicitly expounded upon this, both in principle and in fact, they fully embodied the legacy of the former Buddhas.

Like the sun and moon traversing the heavens or rivers flowing across the earth, it is impossible to feign ignorance of this, lest one deceive oneself and others. Regarding the provisional precepts, one should simply maintain them...

One who possesses the precepts (*śīla*) is unable to advance in the cultivation of the three blessings. One with true precepts (*bhūta-śīla*) maintains the full precepts and further advances in the cultivation of the three blessings, as described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
One with provisional concentration (*upāya-samādhi*) is merely able to recite the Buddha’s name throughout their life but has not yet realized "one mind unmuddled.

One with precious concentration (*ratna-samādhi*) enters retreat and focuses exclusively on recitation, realizing "one mind unmuddled" in the present; internally, they subdue and eliminate [afflictions].
Regarding the two delusions of views and thoughts: externally, one beholds Amitābha Buddha’s adornments of both the Dharma-body and the physical realm, as well as the Buddhas of the ten directions.

As for provisional wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*), it refers to a profound mastery of the various teachings of the Pure Land school regarding faith, understanding, practice, and realization, such that one cannot be shaken or diverted by conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

As for ultimate wisdom (*tattva-prajñā*), it refers to closing the retreat door and focusing single-mindedly until one has realized "one mind without distraction" and attained true meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
