Having practiced without ceasing, and having previously made the vow to realize the nature of one's mind, one subsequently attains a vast and sudden awakening to the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*).
One clearly perceives one’s own fundamental mind and beholds one’s own original nature; this is what is termed "ultimate samādhi" (*jiujing sanmei*).
Ultimate samādhi is precisely what was referred to above as "true wisdom" (*shihui*). Once one has realized this fundamental samādhi, then Amitābha Buddha—

The Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as all the environments and their inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) of the world of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), appear universally before one’s eyes.
Nothing—not even palaces, walls, mountains, rivers, forests, or foothills—can obstruct this.
The world of Ultimate Bliss and this realm merge completely into one, just as described in ancient scriptures such as the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* and various texts of the *Avataṃsaka*. Now...
This is verified by what the Great Master Xingyi realized. Having realized the ultimate samādhi, he beheld Amitābha face-to-face and personally heard him preach the Dharma.
He attained thorough understanding of all the dharma-gates in the various sutras, and his wisdom and eloquence never ceased.
He immediately attained the all-encompassing wisdom of all Buddhas, as recorded in ancient scriptures such as the Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā and the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
If one examines what is set forth in the various scriptures today, it corresponds exactly to what was realized by the Great Master Zhu’an. As for the essence and function of nianfo:
internally, it eliminates falsehood and delusion; externally, it ensures certain rebirth in the Pure Land. This has now been verified and established as a certainty.
Thus, the deluded mind is purified and exhausted; one already holds the talisman for rebirth in the Pure Land at the moment of death.

Having established the foundation, there is progress and no retreat—this is the essential point of samādhi and the auspicious sign of nianfo. Therefore, the first samādhi is regarded as the fundamental samādhi.
Once authentic concentration is realized, if one continues to practice without ceasing, wisdom will arise from that concentration. This is...

This is the natural sequence of all samādhis. Being able to perceive one's own original nature, one naturally and wondrously accords with True Suchness (Tathatā), ascending to the same level as the Buddha’s wisdom;
this constitutes the ultimate limit of samādhi and the supreme achievement of Buddha-recollection.
Therefore, the second samādhi is designated as the ultimate samādhi. Nevertheless, the practitioner must open the gate and observe silence, cultivating with single-minded devotion.
Through practice, one thoroughly restrains the six sense faculties and maintains a continuous stream of pure mindfulness; thus, one attains the full realization of the fundamental samādhi.
Having realized the fundamental samādhi, if one continues to advance in cultivation without ceasing, one will further realize the ultimate samādhi.

If, however, having realized the fundamental samādhi, one does not continue to advance in cultivation, one will inevitably stagnate halfway and be unable to advance to realize the ultimate. It is just as [in the case of]...

consequently, when examining his realization today, it lacks any effect that transcends the mundane. Master Zhuan’an, however, maintained a long retreat period and possessed a firm and resilient resolve;
thus, he attained both concentration and wisdom, ultimately realizing the full perfection of *samādhi*. As for his...

it cannot be faked or glossed over by those who engage in mere empty talk of Prajñā. Since the Yuan and Ming dynasties, the various masters of the Pure Land school have also attempted to examine ancient scriptures from above, yet they have been unable to verify this through present-day evidence. Therefore, regarding the two types of samādhi...

The sequence of names and realities has not been elucidated in any of them. Now, I have synthesized and scrutinized the teachings of the past and present, relying primarily on what I have personally verified, and respectfully set forth this meaning as an offering to those who cultivate true practice and seek authentic realization.

This is indeed the ultimate attainment already expounded by former Buddhas; it is the actual merit realized by the masters Xingxian and Fashu, and is not something that could be produced by my own private intelligence alone.

This was the original opening [of the path]. Now, the contemporary lecturers of secular traditions, fearing difficulty and seeking mere ease, largely treat "shutting the gate and reciting the Buddha's name" as a taboo.

They merely wish to remain leisurely while holding the name, hoping for the fortune of rebirth in the Pure Land. Being of inferior and ignorant understanding, they harmonize with this cry in unison, a hundred voices following one.
Because they have long been accustomed to these practices, they have attained a single school of samādhi through present realization; thus, the study of the Way has nearly become extinct.
This is the profound sorrow of those who cultivate pure karma. However, men of superior faculties and heroic character will certainly not be deluded by worldly customs.
Therefore, I have fully set forth what I know and separately expounded this new method to inform the world and future generations. Those who aspire to the Ultimate Way will surely [understand].
One must certainly have a way to establish oneself.
To close the gates and recite the Buddha’s name is also called the "Dharma-gate of Exclusive Recitation.

This is explained in detail in such scriptures as the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Some commentators claim that this particular sūtra alone lacks the method of exclusive recitation; this is a grave error.

Not so. What is called "single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting Amitābha Buddha" in the sixteenth chapter of the original sutra refers to the method of nianfo (recitation) practiced during both the settled and dispersed periods of daily life.

What is called "sentient beings in this world of five turbidities practicing with diligence for one day and night, or ten days and ten nights" in the nineteenth chapter refers to the practice of seclusion and exclusive recollection.
This is the Dharma. If one does not close the door and practice focused mindfulness (*ekāgratā*), what is there to call "diligence," and how could there be such things as ten days and ten nights?
To forget this and fail to examine it, thereby suspecting that the root scripture lacks the method of focused mindfulness, is most reckless.

For those who cultivate the Pure Land practice, if they rely solely on the two sessions of reciting the Buddha's name—both in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and in distraction (*vikṣepa*)—hoping for the mere chance of rebirth, then [the method of] focused mindfulness...

The Dharma is not something to be merely carried as a gift. If you are truly resolved to aspire upward and desire to authentically cultivate and realize the two kinds of samādhi, thereby fully grasping the talisman for rebirth in the Pure Land and the realization of one's nature, then there are certainly methods for secluding oneself in retreat and single-minded recitation that must be expounded with urgency.

Regarding this, the Great Master Yunqi of recent times did not know that samādhi is to be realized in the present; he insisted instead that it must await seclusion in retreat and single-minded practice.

He then submitted his actual experience. Yet, he remained unaware that the common practice of "shutting the gate" (closed-door retreat) lacked a formal method, which led to the proliferation of errors and delusions;
he even went so far as to mock and criticize closed-door *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).

This reasoning is truly incomprehensible, especially considering he was a master who revitalized the Pure Land school, yet his own views were such that they left the essentials of single-minded recitation nearly without settled doctrine. [Manifest Realization, Part Three]
Obscured. How many have failed to achieve the study of cessation, causing the Pure Land school to decline further and further; this is not at all surprising.
Although the methods for single-minded recitation are explained in great detail, in reality, they consist of nothing more than practicing "doing nothing.
If one cannot practice "doing nothing," one will inevitably create affairs where there are none; this is something I truly dare not even contemplate. As for what is called the "New Method":
There are five essentials and five precepts. As for the five essentials: first, selecting the location; second, selecting the person; third, making a prior agreement; fourth, fixing the date;
and fifth, the ritual procedure. As for the five precepts: first, refraining from speech; second, setting aside worldly affairs.
Third is observing the fast; fourth is declining visitors; fifth is guarding against regression. Yet the supreme essential does not exceed a single matter. This single matter is as follows:
apart from the three matters of eating, drinking, and attending to excretions and sleep, one’s mouth shall only recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing;
one’s mind shall only keep the Buddha in mind without ceasing; and one’s ears shall only listen to the Buddha without ceasing. As for eating and drinking...
When defecating or urinating, although one may not recite the Buddha’s name aloud, one must never fail to keep the Buddha in mind within the heart. It is the same while lying down;
it ceases only when one falls asleep, and upon waking, one resumes again. This is the fixed method for single-minded mindfulness. One does not recite the Buddha’s name aloud.

This is what is meant by external severance. When the mind does not recollect the Buddha, this is what is meant by internal severance. With external severance, there may still be times when one is compelled [to practice];
however, if there is internal severance, the mind is no longer with the Buddha. If the mind is not with the Buddha, how can there be any single-minded mindfulness?

For those who cultivate the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection, although they may isolate themselves from external conditions and recite with single-minded devotion, delusive thoughts still surge forth in their chests in an unending torrent.

If one is first overcome by indolence and cannot restrain the mind in a single point, then the efficacy of single-mindedness will be even more difficult to hope for. This is why practitioners of the Way must value diligent effort (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, regarding the method for selecting a site: one should choose an ancient monastery within a forest community or a secluded garden as the appropriate location.
It must be far removed from the clamor of the marketplace outside and completely free from visitors within, so as to avoid the烦扰 (disturbance) of explanations and discussions.

As for the hall for practicing the Way, it should generally consist of three bays within a detached courtyard. Within these three bays, the western bay shall be designated as the room for making offerings to the Buddha, while the eastern [bay]...
One bay shall serve as the sleeping quarters for the attendant; the central bay shall be used to store miscellaneous items, or may serve as the sleeping quarters for the attendants.
Within the hall where the Buddha is enshrined, one should hang a single scroll of the painting of the Three Sages of the West, or simply enshrine a single golden image of Amitābha Buddha.
The image must face east. On the table before the image, provide only a single incense burner.
In front of the practitioner, there is arranged only a single *bōtuán* (rush mat). When the practitioner sits, they must lean against the eastern wall; when seated, they must face west.

Within the shrine room for making offerings to the Buddha, other than the image’s pedestal, the incense burner, and the *bōtuán*, there are no other objects. This is for the purpose of purifying the eyes and mind.

This is to sever external conditions. Within the sleeping chamber, one should place only the bed, bedding, and pillows, as well as necessary clothing, writing implements (pen, ink, paper, and inkstone), and tea utensils. All books and articles of luxury must be discarded and not kept;
this, too, is for the purpose of severing external conditions. If a portable toilet is not used, then for urination and defecation, one should go outside the courtyard.
The Buddha’s chamber is located in a secluded place; its sweeping and cleaning should have fixed times to avoid the clamor and contention of idle people.
At the main gate outside the courtyard, those in charge of service should descend the bolt from the outside, except for those bringing food, drink, or water for washing.
One must not open [the door] recklessly. Aside from one person assigned to service, others must not be allowed to enter at will.
Each day the door is opened, it should be done only four times as a rule; unless there is an unexpected emergency, one must not open it recklessly.

This is the essential principle of the practice of *kanbō* (shutting the gate). Indeed, the method of single-minded recitation takes the refusal of guests and the prohibition of speech as its foundation.
This is the foremost prudent calculation: do not lower the bolt at the gate.

Should an outsider enter uninvited, and since the traveler is unable to respond due to the vow of silence, it will inevitably cause people to wonder and marvel; thus, one’s own internal afflictions will also increase.
Therefore, one must be especially careful. Regarding the selection of persons, there are two types: first, those who guard the gates; second, those who serve as attendants.
The person guarding the gate is none other than a close friend or fellow practitioner;
their sole duty is to exclude outsiders and ensure that no one enters the chamber uninvited, as well as to prohibit the clamor and bustle of those nearby. There is no other task required.

Nevertheless, it is essential to employ a person of sincerity and integrity, for only then can there be no concern regarding negligence or forgetfulness. Should such negligence occur, unforeseen calamities may arise.
Disturbance is also a great affliction. As for those who perform the service, there should be two at most, or one at least;

they must be sincere and simple, and reliable enough to remain consistent from beginning to end—only such persons may be entrusted with this task. Furthermore, rewards after the work is completed must not be lacking.
The duties consist merely of preparing and delivering food, drink, and bathing water according to a fixed schedule, as well as conveying clothing and urinals, and attending to the matter at hand.
Beyond the aforementioned matters such as the key, there is no cause for weariness.
Nevertheless, one may encounter deceitful and wicked individuals who fail to provide food and drink at the proper times, resulting in hunger where one cannot eat and thirst where one cannot drink;
or they may lose the key, allowing outsiders to enter and needlessly engendering affliction—these too are grave misfortunes. Should such unforeseen circumstances arise, [one must remain vigilant].
If it is necessary to employ an attendant, one should write a note and entrust it to them; this is the purpose for which pen and ink are provided.
Should the practitioner be timid and unable to dwell alone in a quiet room, they may have that person enter the gate at dusk to stay overnight in an outer chamber as a companion.
However, external disturbances can rarely be avoided; in all cases, it is best to remain alone.
Furthermore, there are four stipulations regarding prior commitments. For one who has entered retreat, being free from other entanglements is certainly a superior condition;

however, for others—whether monastics or laypeople—if they have parents, teachers, or elders, should those individuals fall ill during the period of retreat, there is no reason why the retreat should not be broken and one should depart. Alternatively, if the practitioner themselves falls ill...
If one falls ill or encounters unexpected circumstances, there may also be occasions when one cannot help but pass through the frontier station.
Before entering the station, the traveler should instruct their family members and the officials guarding the station in advance:

"In the event that an unexpected situation arises, you must only send a letter specifically requesting permission to exit the station for such-and-such a person on account of such-and-such a matter. As for any other matters whatsoever, [one must not do so].

One must not act with arrogance or make groundless requests, nor cause a disturbance for no reason; this is the first point. When a traveler reaches the pass, they should simply focus their mind on the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

There is absolutely no principle of counting days on one's fingers to calculate the date of departure. If one has already realized single-mindedness (*ekacitta*), the mind will have no other thoughts, and thus one will naturally not know what day the departure from the pass will be.
Even if one has not yet realized single-mindedness, even if the period of stay is too long, it is still [the case].
One must certainly not set a specific date for exiting the pass. Instead, prior to entering the pass, one should first entrust the matter to the attendants;

then, on the day following the expiration of the pass period, one should write a note requesting the traveler to exit the pass. In this way, there will be no anxiety or agitation regarding the counting of days.
This is another matter. Furthermore, the outer gate must remain locked throughout the entire day to avoid intruders from outside.

Uninvited entry must be prevented; those guarding the gates and those on duty must not leave their posts for even a moment throughout the day, for only then can they guard against unexpected disturbances—this is another matter.
Furthermore, food and drink must be delivered at precise times, neither too early nor too late;
the removal of excrement and urine must be performed at precise times, neither too frequently nor too infrequently—this too is another matter.
Indeed. For once the practitioners have been enjoined to observe silence, they can no longer involve themselves in external affairs;

were it not for prior agreements and constraints, they would inevitably resort to pretenses and deceptions at the last moment, which would be impossible to comprehend. Those who serve as attendants are generally of low intelligence and, moreover, rarely possess sincerity.
Therefore, one must admonish them earnestly before the task begins and not stint on rewards after it is completed; only then will they faithfully accept and carry out the instructions.

I still dare not take this for granted. If those on the journey do not know to issue warnings and instead proceed with reckless ignorance, then the indolence and absurdity of such people will surely become beyond reproach; if they do not prepare in advance, they will fail.

This is true even for minor matters, let alone the great task of observing the precept against speaking while reciting the Buddha’s name in order to realize samādhi. Regarding the method of setting a deadline, there are several points. First:
It is said there are two types of periods: the small period and the great period. The small period is established for those who are practicing samādhi as a trial;
the great period is established for those who are correctly practicing samādhi. Regarding the method of single-minded recollection, setting a specific time limit is especially the pivotal point.

For beginners who do not yet know the method of closing the gate (shutting themselves in retreat), fearing the possibility of error, it is permissible to first set a small period to practice. Thus one cultivates.
Once the practice is fully mastered, one may then set a longer term, so that there will be no further doubt or stagnation.
The shorter term varies from ten days at minimum to twenty or thirty days at maximum; as for the longer term, it should be fixed at one hundred and twenty days.

[The opponent] considers the period to be too long, fearing the risks of severe cold and intense heat. Yet, if the period were somewhat shorter, it would not suffice as a basis for manifest realization.
A long term of one hundred and twenty days may fall either between spring and summer, or between autumn and winter.
During spring and summer, it should be during the second, third, fourth, or perhaps the second, third, and fourth months, with the fourth month being [the limit].
Regarding the seasonal periods: in autumn and winter, they should be the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth months; or alternatively, the eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh.
The fourth month serves as the seasonal boundary (*jié*). Beyond this point, one has already entered either the severe cold or the humid heat.

Within the closed quarters of the monastery, it is neither permissible to be naked before the Buddha nor convenient to surround oneself with braziers and glowing coals, as both would give rise to excessive external disturbances. Therefore, these two periods must certainly be established as the fixed times.
Furthermore, the physical bodies of practitioners also possess varying degrees of strength or weakness.

For instance, a person of frail constitution may, after practicing recitation for as long as one hundred and twenty days, inevitably suffer from the ailment of physical debility; this can be remedied by taking advantage of the two seasons of severe cold and intense heat.
This is to nourish the physical constitution and to restore the spirit, thereby establishing a foundation for courageous and diligent practice in the future.
If one does not understand this principle, progress will inevitably be swift at first but retreat rapid thereafter, which would instead undermine the sincerity of cultivation.

This teaching is specifically established for those of middling or inferior capacity, as well as for those whose external conditions are incomplete; however, it is not so for practitioners of superior roots who seek the Way.
Disregarding their own lives and bodies, indifferent to cold and heat, they advance with courageous determination, never wavering or becoming indolent;
those who vow that realization must be attained as their immediate goal are surely not non-existent. Masters such as Duanzhuan (澍庵) of recent times are precisely of this caliber.
This matter cannot be constrained by ordinary deadlines nor measured by those of middling or inferior capacity; it depends solely upon—
It is simply a matter of the practitioner examining themselves. There are two ritual procedures: first, the dedication of merit and the making of vows;
second, maintaining [the practice] without loss. Regarding the meaning of making vows, there are both general and specific types.

Vows such as repentance, the aspiration to be born in the Pure Land, and the arousal of the great mind of bodhicitta—those already spoken of by the ancients—are considered general examples. These are to be personally formulated by the practitioner.
Aspirations (praṇidhāna) constitute a distinct category. If one’s resolve is sincere and earnest, whether the aspiration is general or specific, it can be fulfilled according to one's wishes.

If the resolve is not sincere and earnest, even if there is a specific aspiration, it remains mere empty words without benefit. Furthermore, regarding those who formulate their own specific aspirations:
One must first master the scriptural teachings so that the vows one makes are entirely in accord with perfect enlightenment; only then can one avoid falling into error.
If one does not understand the meaning of the teachings and recklessly makes vows that should not be made, it is better simply to direct one's merit through the "Universal Vow" (Tongyuan).
Apart from the Universal Vow, if one makes specific vows, let them be solely for the purpose of repenting the transgressions of one’s parents.

Seeking blessings is deeply in accord with the meaning of the teachings; it is highly capable of yielding results. All other practices should take the universal vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*) as their primary focus.
If one harbors erroneous views, or falsely hopes for supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the like, such as the ability to know the future, this constitutes the teaching of Pāpīyān.

It is a great precept for those who practice correctly that one must not fail to be cautious in this regard. Among the texts concerning the universal vow, those that are both extensive and refined include the *Yun* (Cloud) [Sutra].
Regarding Master Xi’s *Vow Text for Rebirth in the Western Land*, that which is concise yet essential is the *Vow Gāthā for Nianfo* by the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitreya.
One should focus one’s recitation and dedicate the merit, taking this vow text as the primary guide.

On the first day of the practitioner’s entry into the retreat enclosure, they should first carefully transcribe the vow text upon yellow paper. Having burned incense and paid homage to the Buddha, they should immediately [place it] before the Buddha in the fire.
After performing the transformation, follow the ritual for the regular daily recitation as listed above.
First recite the name of our Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, and proceed in order until reaching the "Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean Assembly.

Then, once more recite the prayer text one time aloud, after which withdraw to sit and recollect the Buddha. From this point forward, for the next one hundred and twenty days, devote yourself exclusively each day to [this practice].
Recite the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha without further entangling the mind in other thoughts or matters, continuing until one exits the retreat.

This is the ritual for making vows on the first day of a closed-door retreat dedicated to exclusive recitation. The text of the Vows for the Western Pure Land is profound and comprehensive in its meaning;
it serves for all who repent of karma to seek rebirth, arouse the bodhicitta, and realize the fundamental [nature] in the present life.
Having thoroughly mastered the various meanings of the two kinds of samādhi, there is nothing that is not fully possessed.

When a practitioner enters the "gate" (the period of intensive practice) with single-minded mindfulness and employs this text for dedication, they should simply add the phrase "may I be empowered" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) within the text and delete the nine characters consisting of the two phrases "within dhyāna-contemplation" and "during the time of dreams.
Furthermore, one should separately increase the phrase "I pray that for one hundred and twenty days... at the end of the "gate."
Within this period, he directly attained single-mindedness and subsequently realized samādhi. He further reported that he had come to behold Amitābha Buddha, and so forth.
Regarding the specific aspirations he sought while in retreat through exclusive recitation (*ekāgrasmṛti*), there was nothing that was not fulfilled.

However, those who wish to practice the dharma-gate of exclusive recitation must first take up this text for study until they are thoroughly proficient; only then will the vows contained within the text be realized as one’s own.
Whatever one’s heart desires, if one can indeed maintain it without loss, it will naturally lead, through gradual cultivation, to spiritual resonance.
If one does not understand the subtlety of its meaning and intent, it is no different from having no aspiration at all; this must be understood.

However, this is said for those who are able to comprehend the words and texts. As for those who do not understand the meaning of the text, they know only that there is the direct realization of focused recitation.
Regarding the Dharma: when entering the cloistered retreat (*kuan*), one should simply pay homage to the Buddha and offer silent prayers, seeking only that the mind remain undistracted.
Once one has actually beheld the Buddha face-to-face, then all other meanings are inherently encompassed; there is no need to cling to the wording of the prayer.
For the method of the retreat takes the resolute determination and single-minded recollection as its primary principle; everything else cannot avoid being secondary. This...
Furthermore, there is one thing you must not fail to know: the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation is the foremost matter for attaining the supramundane, ultimate Way.
To close oneself in retreat and recite with single-minded devotion in order to seek manifest realization is the primary method of Buddha-recitation.

Since it is called "single-minded recitation," it consists solely in maintaining the practice without losing it; there are no other ritual procedures. However, as for maintaining it without loss, its essential meaning is profound.

Furthermore, there exists a ritual within the absence of ritual. Therefore, when eating and drinking, though one cannot recite the Buddha’s name with the mouth, if one continues to recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing in the mind, this is itself the ritual.

When defecating or urinating, though it is not necessary to recite the Buddha’s name with the mouth, if one continues to recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing in the mind, this too is the ritual. When ascending the bed to lie down, though it is not necessary with the mouth—
To recite the Buddha’s name while maintaining an uninterrupted mindfulness of the Buddha within the mind is also a ritual procedure.
To ensure that there is no interval between heart and mouth where one is not mindful of the Buddha is also a ritual procedure. Within the Buddha-chamber, only the practitioner alone may enter;
even those who perform manual labor are not permitted to enter—this too is a ritual procedure. When sitting, regardless of...
One may sit either in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) or in a seated posture; either is permissible, provided one does not lean to one side or neglect reverence—this is also a rule of decorum.

When weary from sitting, it is not forbidden to perform circumambulation before the Buddha; however, one must walk slowly and with composure, and must not stride hurriedly or neglect reverence—this is also a rule of decorum.
One must not wear short-sleeved garments within the Buddha chamber—this is also a rule of decorum. At night...

When lying down, one should only remove the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*); it is not permitted to remove both the inner robe (*antarvāsaka*) and the undergarment (*nivasana*) at once. This is also a rule of decorum.

As for rising, one should do so at the fifth watch of the night at the earliest, or at dawn at the latest. Those who are prone to heavy sleep may go to bed early without hindrance, but they must not rise late.

This is also a ritual rule. One must not sleep during the daytime; this is also a ritual rule. Prior to entering the retreat enclosure (*kuan*), one should bathe and change clothes to demonstrate purity.
During the period of the retreat, one must not again bathe as it would interfere with one's practice; this is also a ritual rule.
During the period of the retreat, one must not pass the time by reading books, nor may one linger in the outer courtyard or sleep there.

To occupy oneself with writing in one's quarters is also a rule of decorum. During the period of confinement, unless there is a matter of great importance, one must not entrust letters to those outside;

to occupy oneself with writing is likewise a rule of decorum. During the period of confinement, except for burning incense and prostrating before the Buddha to offer prayers on the first day, and burning incense and prostrating before the Buddha upon the completion of the period before finally withdrawing, one should otherwise do nothing but [meditate] each day.

When entering the retreat chamber at dawn, one should perform one prostration to the Buddha. While there is no fixed number for prostrations at other times, it is not necessary to burn incense on those occasions;
this too is part of the ritual protocol. During regular daily recitations of the Buddha’s name, one should always use a prayer bead to keep count.
However, during the exclusive recitation of the retreat, one must not use beads to count, as doing so would increase external distractions; this too is part of the ritual protocol. This...
This is the ritual for those who have no rituals. That which the Buddha entrusts to sentient beings depends solely upon a single mind free from distraction.

That by which sentient beings close their gates to recite the Buddha’s name also depends solely upon completely setting aside external conditions, hoping to achieve, even if only slightly, the realization of a single mind free from distraction.
This is the primary meaning of exclusive mindfulness. If one does not know this...
Regarding this principle: some take veneration of the Buddha as true respect, yet do not realize that single-minded mindfulness is true respect;

others take ritual bathing as true purity, yet do not realize that single-minded mindfulness is true purity. Thus, they contradict the bequeathed teachings of the Buddhas of the past above, and turn their backs on the authentic practice of single-minded mindfulness below.
They have already incurred the fault of prioritizing formalities while neglecting the underlying principle. If one calls this "closing the gate" (confinement retreat), yet...
To be willing to decline visitors yet unwilling to refrain from speech is to treat the diligent recitation of the sublime Dharma as a mere pastime;
such a person is utterly unworthy of being consulted on this matter. This, moreover, is a fundamental principle and grand purport within the practice of exclusive recitation.
As for what is called "refraining from speech": after entering the inner sanctuary, this mouth must not utter any words other than the Buddha’s name. This is what is meant by...
Regarding the prohibitions: after entering the enclosure, this body may not engage in any other affairs besides the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.

If one does not understand this principle—that it constitutes the entire essence and great function of nianfo by holding the name—one lacks true and clear insight;
even if one were to falsely practice visualization, nothing at all would be gained. To enter deeply through a single gate is the orthodox tradition of studying the Way. This is the practice.
The essential key to realization is this: if one practices three in the morning and four in the evening, how can such a person speak of the Ultimate Way?

This is the error of clinging to visualized contemplation. The true efficacy of Buddha-recitation lies solely in single-mindedness without distraction. If one realizes this single-mindedness, it constitutes true samādhi;
thus, regarding the transcendence of the world, one will certainly attain the two types of samādhis—prior and subsequent manifestation—in the highest grade.

He was reborn in the higher realms, transcending the cycle of birth and death and the myriad things with effortless ease. To say that he governed the world through his teachings is to mean that all evils were swept away like lightning and all virtues gathered like clouds.
He held a preeminent position among the four categories of disciples in the Confucian school and simultaneously attained the three forms of immortality established by the House of Shusun.
Famous ministers and upright officials were all but the remnants of this [teaching], achieved without the need for strenuous effort.
To speak of "immortality" (xian), one could attain definitive transcendence at will; yet those who have profoundly understood the nature of birth and death have no further use for such transcendence.

For when the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are exhausted, the various delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*), dust, and sand must necessarily be gradually eliminated in their proper sequence; it cannot be otherwise.

This is insufficient to realize ultimate samādhi. Yet, if one wishes to realize these various samādhis simultaneously, there is no other skillful means than the method of secluding oneself in retreat and focusing single-mindedly on recitation.
Fools, however, fail to perceive this; they instead engage in ritualistic repentance (*sāmtāpana-karma*), thereby obscuring true cultivation.

Moreover, some mistakenly take such ritualistic repentance to be true cultivation—is this not a laughingstock? This is because they lack a profound understanding of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding this profound source, whenever I encounter various rituals for the Pure Land repentance and vows, I cannot help but sigh with deep regret.
Thus, those who aspire to realize samādhi must simply remain in seclusion and focus their mindfulness exclusively; anything else is not worth mentioning.
This is the error of being attached to ritualistic repentance. To penetrate the fundamental principles of nianfo (Buddha-recitation), one must first possess thorough understanding.

Regarding the fundamental principles of the various schools—Chan, Teaching (Dharma), Vinaya, and Esoteric—one must first possess a thorough mastery of the four categories and three forms of immortality of the sages who governed the world.
Furthermore, one must first possess a thorough mastery of the principles of investigating things and extending knowledge.
Yet these several points cannot possibly be attained without first reading the classics and subsequently attending to teachers and seeking out friends; this is not a matter of mere effort.

It is absolutely impossible for one who harbors heterodox views regarding the gateway [to the Dharma] to attain this; nor is it absolutely possible for one who has not first possessed a will that integrates both good [traditions].

If one relies solely on the single treatise or single doctrine of ordinary lecturers, or rejects them through the empty talk of Confucian and Daoist practitioners, there are few who do not fall under their delusion. This is because even among the various schools of the Pure Land tradition...
In this writing, even those points that appear shallow or crude should not be accepted uncritically; other matters may be inferred from this.
This is why it is difficult to achieve a comprehensive synthesis and thorough understanding, and why one must be cautious when following what is superficial or adopting what is expedient.

Thus, if one truly wishes to enter this community of the protected, how could they be mere pedants confined to sectarian gateways, ignorant monks or Daoists, or those who merely seek to satisfy their appetites and please themselves?
Those who merely seek to preserve their physical bodies, families, and wives—what have they truly attained? This is the error of adhering to the vulgar and the simplistic.
The *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi) is the crown jewel among all forms of samādhi.
It alone synthesizes the excellences of both worldly and world-transcending practices; therefore, it serves as the crown for all other samādhis, presiding over them like a royal diadem.
The common run of people now wishes to shake this with a frivolous mind, yet they constantly maintain it in the hope of seeking signs and verification—is this possible?

The preceding section on the Dharma-gate of Exclusive Recollection was written by me after extensively examining the scriptures of the Buddhas of the past and personally beholding the Great Beings who have attained true cultivation and actual realization;
furthermore, I have myself experienced firsthand the gains and losses of such true cultivation and realization. It is for these reasons that I venture to disregard criticism and suspicion.

I have set forth in detail what I have observed. This is my wish to announce widely to the virtuous and benevolent men of the world and future generations, and my hope that the heterodox teachings and deviant practices of the world throughout all ages may be entirely stilled.
Indeed, this is a discourse of universal verification, free from delusion, in accordance with the Buddhas.
However, if there were no such person, the Way would not manifest in vain. Reflecting upon myself, I see that my decline and illness encroach daily, yet I remain entangled in the worldly net;

I can no longer advance to realize the ultimate perfection of samādhi, for which I feel deep self-reproach. If the exposition of this teaching is to be precise, thorough, and illuminating, it is certainly no easy matter.
Indeed, in this world, there must truly exist a hero who is proficient in both the mundane and the supramundane.

Excellent! You should know that to transcend the cycle of birth and death within the realm of segmentation (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*), there is no method other than this for transforming from the mundane into the sacred.
May you exert yourself in authentic cultivation to further seek the realization of samādhi in this very life; thus, you will be sufficient to serve as a model for humans and devas.
Furthermore, one may fully equip oneself with the six perfections and myriad practices to universally rescue all sentient beings; this serves as a clear proof for my humble discourse.

If you do not examine my sincere heart of compassion, but instead merely desire to vainly hope for samādhi through the method of avoiding difficulty for ease, or if you fail to consult ancient scriptures above and verify present evidence below, engaging instead in empty talk that neglects the reality of practice.

If the transmission for realizing this meaning were not made manifest in the world, such that people would deceive themselves and others, leading one another to drown, there would be nothing that could be done about it.
I previously composed a verse on the Sudden and Gradual Approaches to Buddha-Recitation, which says: "To practice the gradual without practicing the sudden..."
Without means, one cannot realize samādhi; the power of karma continues to entangle. The power of the Path does not easily retreat. One may practice both suddenly and gradually;
by slaying the enemy, one expects to attain the fruit. Tread upon the reality and abandon empty talk; all Buddhas will approve this. If one practices neither the sudden nor the gradual, [one fails].
Those who remain complacent in ignorance lack virtuous planning; they do not understand how to transcend saṃsāra and will ultimately be subject to the constraints of the three miserable realms.

By practicing both the sudden and gradual approaches, one perceives the Buddha and realizes one's own nature, appearing as a teacher of devas and humans, and finally returning to the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

This distinction between the sudden and gradual aspects of nianfo is also the difference between the gains and losses of avoiding difficulty to pursue ease. Such is the explanation of the ten errors, even according to the original sutra.
These are merely redundant words. They represent the definitive meaning of the true Dharma-realm; thus, even though they may be rejected by the sages of yore, I do not decline to speak them.
It is not that I delight in disputation, but rather that I have no other choice.

The old *Biographies of the Great Master Shengyi* states: The Great Master Shengyi’s personal name has not been recorded in historical examinations. His secular surname was Gao; he was a native of Jiangdu in Yangzhou.
His family had been farmers for generations, yet the Master was particularly upright and sincere. At the age of twelve, he observed the mourning period for his mother.
He grieved and emaciated himself without ceasing, thinking that a person cannot do without a mother; indeed, without a mother, one cannot even be considered human.

From this, he conceived the aspiration for the transcendent life (*lokottara*), but it was not realized because his father obstructed him. When he reached the age of nineteen, his father also passed away.

He then entered the Tiantong Peak Temple (*Tianfeng si*) to shave his head and dye his robes, subsequently receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) at the Tianning Temple in Yangzhou. During his childhood, he had once heard...
People said, "All who leave the household life shall surely attain the supreme fruit. He took this to heart with deep joy.

Once he had left the household life, he repeatedly sought the methods for cultivation and practice, but found no one who knew them. After a long time, he first heard of the Pure Land teachings from a monk at Mount Jiao.

He immediately established his own course of study and devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name without ceasing. After several more years, someone again informed him of the method of seeking rebirth by fixing a specific deadline.

When he attained the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, the Master rejoiced and said, "It must be thus that it is called 'Perfect and Sudden. Otherwise, one would merely remain in a state of stagnation for a lifetime;
what would be the point? He then made a vow to retreat into seclusion for one hundred and twenty days to recite the Buddha's name, vowing to realize the samādhi through direct manifestation.
Once he had entered the retreat, delusive thoughts arose in profusion, surging and churning without ceasing. When the period was complete, there was nothing [attained].

He attained it. The Master was deeply grieved and planned to attempt it again, vowing that he would not stop until he had certainly achieved it. After several more years, he again entered retreat at Yangzhou.

At the beginning of his practice, his various delusions were as they had been before; even after fifty days, they still had not ceased. The Master was greatly distressed and applied himself with even greater earnestness.
After twenty-odd days of this, he turned back to observe his own mind and mental states, perceiving that his emotional consciousness had been shattered and his deluded thoughts [dissolved].
His breathing gradually subsided, and his mind was somewhat comforted. After a long while, he became aware of the disturbance of deluded thoughts occurring no more than three or five times a day;
immediately, he saw Amitābha Buddha standing upright in the midst of space, His golden countenance radiant, His adornments subtle and wondrous, beyond description.
Having prostrated, the Master thought to himself: "The Buddha is already before me; it is inconvenient to urinate, defecate, lie down, or sleep."
"What can be done? After a moment, he said with a sense of clarity: "If even one's parents do not shrink from the impurities of their own children, how much less so the Buddha?

From this point on, he practiced with courageous diligence, and his recitations became increasingly devout. After a long time, his mind and its objects became vast and empty, identical to the great void.
Good thoughts, evil thoughts, and even subtle, miscellaneous discursive thoughts vanished without a trace. Whether in motion or stillness, his mind remained as one.
At the opening of his mouth, nothing remained but the name of the Buddha; even when he sought out deluded thoughts, they were utterly unobtainable.
Reaching this state, his spirit and vital energy were doubly full; he no longer slept, nor did he feel hunger or thirst. When food arrived, he ate it without any sense of suffering.
As for external objects, they were transparently luminous; the Land of Ultimate Bliss and this world merged into one. The walls of the room where he resided were all...

Hidden within, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fill the great void. There are golden grounds, lotus ponds, rows of trees made of the seven treasures, and palaces and towers reaching from the sky to the earth;

those visible to the eye are beyond counting. Wherever they walk or sit, the environment is uniform, radiating light without interruption, such that day and night cannot be distinguished. Its transcendent excellence and vast splendor far surpass those of many pure lands.
Because it was not covered by the sutras, he was unable to recognize them all. One day, while he was engaged in recitation, he saw two precious lotus flowers before him.
Upon each flower sat a celestial being whose appearance was identical to that of the bodhisattvas, yet their spirit resembled his parents.
As soon as he cast a glance at them, one of the beings had already walked slowly to his side; it was indeed his mother. She spoke joyfully to the Master, saying: "You..."

"It was because of me that you resolved to leave the home life and become a monk. Now that you have realized the Way, both I and your father have been enabled to transcend birth and attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Now, by the Buddha’s command, I have come specifically to comfort you. Just as the Master was about to rise, his mother stopped him, saying:
"The Buddha is right here before you. Do not, for my sake, disturb your power of meditative concentration. Your aspiration is already fulfilled;

we shall meet again in the Pure Land on a future day. Having spoken thus, he vanished. When she looked again at the precious lotus, it was intermingled with the many flowers covering the great earth, and she was so bewildered that she could no longer discern its location.
Since attaining self-realization through samādhi, her mental state and the pure realm have remained unchanging.

He did not retreat, continuing until the full term had expired and he was released from confinement. The Master said, "While I was in confinement, my mind and body were in a state of profound stillness;
I was unaware of the passage of time. Once I had emerged, looking back upon that period, it had been no less than twenty days.
When the Master realized *samādhi*, he was nearly thirty years of age. Thereafter, though he became a man of non-action, he spent his days reciting the Buddha’s name and translating the scriptures.

He never grew weary of his own practice. Having grown old, both his eyebrows and hair were completely white, yet his complexion remained warm and radiant, and his countenance was dignified and imposing.

To those who came to pay their respects, he spoke only of the causal conditions for entering the Way and the realms of realization he had attained. He would frequently admonish people, saying: "Be sincere in your recitation of the Buddha's name;
the Buddha will not deceive you. He further said: "If one truly realizes samādhi, rebirth [in the Pure Land] can be taken as certain. However...
If one cannot close the gates of the senses and restrain speech, there is no way to realize samādhi through single-minded recitation.
When questioned about Chan or the teachings, he would invariably decline, saying he did not know. His instruction of others was thus utterly free from artifice;

consequently, whenever those of empty pretension met the Master face-to-face, they were invariably left despondent and humbled. At over sixty years of age, the Master once served as the abbot of Tianning Temple.
He took his leave of the monastic assembly at the temple. On the sixth day of the fourth month in the eleventh year of the Guangxu era, he passed away at Zhulin Temple in Dantu.
His stupa is located at the foot of Qīnglong Hill on Mount Jia. He was seventy-four years of age and fifty-five years of *dharma-lakṣa* (years of ordination).
The eulogy states: "The power of karma has long been more formidable than the power of the Way; yet those in the world who cultivate the Pure Land..."
To merely recite the name with a distracted mind while hoping to escape birth and death—is this not strange? In the past, I had long heard of the Great Master’s reputation.
It was not until the spring of the seventh year of the Guangxu era that I was finally able to pay my respects at Jinghui Temple in Yangzhou.
The Great Master exhorted me earnestly, as if considering me someone capable of being taught. Although I have since followed his oral instructions to a considerable extent...
I have exhorted myself, yet what I have realized is but slight and shallow; it is insufficient for me to look up to and succeed his lofty footsteps, which fills me with constant shame.

Nevertheless, regarding that which the Great Master entrusted to me, I have held it fast in my heart without forgetting. I still hoped that by striving with diligence until the end of my days, I might surely find one opportunity to repay his kindness;
yet the Great Master has already passed away before such a time could come. As for the single school of the Pure Land, from its establishment at Mount Lu...

Now, some five thousand years have passed. Those who have merely reached its outer fringes are beyond counting, yet those who seek a true cultivation and actual realization like that of the Great Master—one who has established a paradigm for a hundred generations—are exceedingly rare to encounter. This is because empty words and practical realization cannot coexist;
they are mutually exclusive. Indeed, the study of transcendence is none other than the study of treading upon reality. Within the Dharma-gate...
Essentially, nothing surpasses the Pure Land; regarding the essentials of the Pure Land, nothing surpasses seclusion behind closed doors (*yanguan*) while holding the Name.

To realize samādhi in the present life has been clearly demonstrated through a comprehensive examination of the scriptures, leaving no room for doubt. Yet, throughout the ages, the patriarchs and masters have never proposed this as a practice—this is truly the foremost deficiency in the path of perfect enlightenment.
Now the Great Master has arisen to revitalize it; his merit in forging and refining the Dharma-realm is indeed immeasurable.
Regarding this inconceivable matter, I, [the author], shall not presume to judge from without. I have traced back the historical facts at a distance and verified them against what I have heard.

Out of reverence, I compose this biography to serve as an example for future students. Those within the realm who practice the Pure Land path—if they do not wish to cause their own spirits to sink into ruin—should take this as their standard.
If one should say otherwise, I request that you verify it with Śākyamuni, Amitābha, and the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Buddha said, "This is not something known by others. Now, examining what the Great Master realized, it was the fundamental samādhi.

Fundamental samādhi is what is called true concentration (*samāhita*). If, having already attained fundamental samādhi, one further pursues cultivation, then wisdom will arise from that concentration, and one will inevitably advance to realize ultimate samādhi.
It is a pity that the Great Master did not consult the scriptural canons, but instead [proceeded] with this...
This serves to establish the objective sphere (*ālambana*). The fundamental samādhi is like the "breaking through the original barrier" (*ben-can*) in the Chan school;

however, its power of concentration is even deeper and its benefit is even more vast. This is because merely breaking through the original barrier only constitutes the initial foundation of the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*);

its concentration is extremely brief and is insufficient for directly transcending birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Once one has realized the fundamental samādhi through the practice of Buddha-recitation (*nien-fo*), the internal sphere first...

Having already achieved complete purification, one attains the purity of the mind and the Pure Land; externally, one beholds the various Buddhas and the Western Pure Land, thereby grasping the talisman for rebirth there.
Compared to those in the Chan school who strive to break through the barrier of doubt, the difference between success and failure is vast and absolute. This is the first present-day verification.
The old biography of Master Zhuan-’an states: Master Zhuan-’an was a native of Ganquan in Jiangnan;
some say he was from Yizheng, but this cannot be verified in detail. In his youth, he was coarse, unruly, and lacked moral restraint, nor did he observe the precepts.

He once resided at Chansi Temple in Yangzhou, where he quarreled with the head cook, using foul language and behaving discourteously. The presiding monk became enraged and rebuked him before the assembly, and furthermore—
He said, "If you do not reform quickly, you shall be expelled with the summer and winter canes. The Master was filled with resentment and thought of ways to take revenge on the presiding monk.
In the middle of the night, he suddenly repented, saying, "Even if what I am doing could take revenge on the presiding monk, what would I do about the ghosts and spirits?

He then considered a method to wash away his shame, realizing it lay solely in self-cultivation; yet, when looking within himself, he found he lacked any means for the Way of Learning. Thereupon, he...

As the night turned toward dawn, he suddenly attained awakening and said, "I have heard that those who maintain the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī with a sincere heart will all penetrate the source of the Dharma and realize the supreme fruit.
Although I am without knowledge, I am still able to recite this; why should I obstruct myself by claiming I lack the skill?
The next day, he visited the abbot to offer his thanks and declared his wish to close himself in retreat for three years to focus exclusively on maintaining the dhāraṇī.
He recited mantras and requested a quiet room, asking for assistance with the costs of food and clothing. The presiding monk was pleased and granted his request.
The Master then moved to the Tripitaka Library, where he recited the scriptures morning and night without ceasing. He hung a signboard from his chest upon which was written: "Silence.

Whenever anyone ascended the library and wished to speak with him, he would immediately point to the board to show them. After three years had passed, he finally emerged. Once he had come out, his spirit...
His conduct was exceptionally refined; he was humble and self-effacing, such that all who saw him revered and marveled at him, yet none could fathom the level of realization he had attained.
In the custom of Yangzhou, people were fond of drinking tea; tea societies were always full of guests, and the Master would occasionally visit them as well.

At that time, within the realm, the study of textual verification was in vogue. A guest who had been analyzing doubtful points in the classics and scriptures by the Master’s side found his mutual explanations and refutations to be extremely arduous.
The Master smiled but remained silent. When the guest asked for the reason, the Master said, "In all that you gentlemen discuss, there are omissions and errors;
why do you trouble yourselves with such refutations? The guest requested an explanation, and the Master immediately recited for him each of the books they had been debating. Furthermore—

He would recite and explain them with such eloquence and without ceasing that his guests looked at one another in awe and admiration. From this, the Master became renowned for his extensive mastery of the classics.
Among the scholar-officials, there was not a single day when those seeking instruction in the Confucian scriptures and histories did not come to him.

After some time, it became known that regarding all written works—whether internal or external, from the nine schools and hundred masters down to minor tales and short treatises—the Master required no prior visual inspection to master them.

There was no scripture he could not recite from memory. When frivolous youths attempted to test him with texts written in ornate rhetoric, the Master would likewise recite them instantly without hesitation.
Because of this, his spiritual wonders were widely circulated, and he was acclaimed as a "holy monk" (shengseng). At that time, Mr.

Ruan Wenda of Yizheng, who had recently retired from office to live at home, heard of the Master’s reputation and tested him by engaging in conversation; the Master responded tirelessly to every inquiry. Wenda...
He marveled at this, saying, "What the Master has realized is transcendent, far beyond the realm of humans and devas; it is not something that those who merely pore over their books can fathom.
In the Xianfeng era, the Master was already old and infirm, yet he still went out occasionally to receive guests.

Whenever he saw youths playing and sporting without restraint, he would sigh and say, "The younger generation does not practice the right vocation, but devotes themselves only to idle play. The old monk is about to die."
"You shall not see him again. Before long, calamity will arrive; I do not know how you lot will manage to escape it.
Some youths retorted with sharp words, but the Master remained somber and gave no answer. Two years later, the Guangxi rebels fell upon Yangzhou.

It had been more than a year since the Master passed away, yet his words were proven true. In his later years, the Master lived in seclusion, devoting himself solely to the task of transcribing scriptures.

I have personally seen the remaining volumes of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that he transcribed; I have heard that what he transcribed was vast in quantity, with some copies preserved among the monastic communities of Yangzhou.
In praise [of this work], it is said: "The Great Compassion Dhāraṇī possesses a majestic and radiant power that encompasses the entire Dharma-realm."
Regarding both mundane and supramundane learning, there is nothing it does not encompass. Among the ancients who maintained its recitation, there were numerous verified testimonies.
The excellent methods and sublime principles contained in its fundamental scriptures are as clear as the sun and stars;

yet, the ignorant masses of the current age are unable to investigate ancient texts above or verify contemporary evidence below, regarding it merely as a tool for averting calamities and warding off malevolent spirits—how erroneous this is!
The Great Master, starting from the level of inferior ordinary beings, suddenly ascended to the realm of the sages.

Examining what he attained, it was clear that none who had not exhausted the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and fully realized the ultimate fruit of a Śrāvaka could reach this state. At that time, people only recognized his spiritual power but did not understand the reason for that spiritual power;
consequently, there were none who heard of his reputation and were inspired to rise up in emulation. Thus, one can truly believe that those of superior wisdom do not [wait for external conditions].
His spiritual prowess was constant and difficult to encounter. One such as the Great Master—could he not truly be called a dragon or elephant of the Dharma, a resolute and great man?
Shi Xiangkai of Jiangdu, who once studied under the Great Master, often told me that he had seen the Master when he was young.
I have never dared to look up at him; thus, I have had no means to be nourished by the milk of the Dharma to seek liberation for myself.
To this day, I harbor this regret. Alas! For those who seek the Way, there is no other artifice than single-minded devotion.
If one harbors an unyielding resolve, then the established rules of the Great Master remain fully intact—what cause for regret could there be? Now, I shall examine what the Great Master realized.
The Samādhi of Ultimate Perfection. The Samādhi of Finality. This refers to true wisdom. The Great Compassion Dhāraṇī was spoken by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
In past kalpas, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara had already completed his career as a Buddha;
yet, because his vow to deliver sentient beings has no end, he now manifests again as the attendant on the left of Amitābha Buddha in the Western Pure Land.

Therefore, those who uphold this dhāraṇī—whether they concurrently cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, or aspire for rebirth in a pure land—will all realize the fruit of their practice provided they possess true cultivation.
Its efficacy is no different from that of Buddha-recitation (nienfo), as detailed in the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī Sūtra*;
it need not be discussed here in full. The Great Master devoted himself to its recitation for as long as three years, until he finally attained realization through meditative concentration.
As for wisdom, one directly realizes the highest grade of samādhi. Whether or not one is reborn [in a pure land] depends upon one's vows and dedications, which cannot be definitively determined;

yet, the realization itself is such that one has already transcended the cycle of birth and death within the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃvṛti-jāti-maraṇa*), leaving no need for further inquiry.
Ultimate samādhi is like the thorough awakening of the Chan school, yet what is realized therein is even more transcendent.
This is precisely what is shown in the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*. This constitutes the second of the present proofs; it is the entirety of samādhi.
This concludes the sixth section of the central treatise.

Someone asked: "Regarding the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, there are accounts of setting a period of seven days and nights, or a period of forty-nine days, to see the Buddha in this very life.
These explanations should be identical to the text of the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*.

Why, then, do you alone claim that the 'seven days' in the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* refers to a fixed, definitive period [for rebirth], rather than a period for the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation)? The answer was: "The *Pratyutpanna*..."

In the *Zhōuzhì wén* (Text on the Boat), what is emphasized first is mindfulness with a single mind (*ekacitta*). In the *Dàjí wén* (Text on the Great Assembly), what is emphasized first is focused mindfulness (*ekāgrasmṛti*).

For one who shuts the door to cultivate samādhi, if they can recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind and focus their heart entirely on the Buddha’s name, deluded thoughts will naturally subside and single-mindedness will easily be realized.
Regardless of whether it takes seven weeks, one may see the Buddha even in seven days.
Even during the brief period of night, it is not that one cannot see the Buddha. This is the true meaning and the actual reality of the purification of the mind and the purification of the land;

it is no false teaching. It is simply that the various delusions of view and thought are the root of the deluded thoughts of sentient beings, and they are also the foundation for the segmented birth and death of sentient beings.
Sentient beings currently take these deluded thoughts of view and thought to be their reality.

I have abandoned these [distractions], yet for some time there has been no place of rest. This is why deluded thoughts are not easily exhausted and why the true concentration of mindfulness of the Buddha is not easily accomplished.

Unless one is a gentleman of genuine cultivation and realization who has investigated things to the utmost and attained knowledge, one can never fathom the profound subtleties of right and wrong herein; yet the secular world currently regards mindfulness of the Buddha as...
This matter of being "easy to practice and easy to realize" is so absurd that it can hardly be reconciled with reason; it is truly laughable.

Thus, although the various *Pratyutpanna* sutras contain passages regarding fixed periods such as seven days and nights, these are not actually achievable undertakings for the vast majority of sentient beings.
Those who study the Way, wishing to seek truth from facts and to truly realize samādhi, must not cling to such [misconceptions].

These surviving texts deceive themselves. As for the text of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, it clearly establishes seven days as the period for remaining in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), not the period for reciting the Buddha’s name.
A careful reading of the original text leaves no room for doubt; this has already been examined in detail.
There is no need to cling to the text of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* to forcibly raise objections, thereby misleading sentient beings regarding the true nature of concentration and wisdom.

This is an emulation. Someone asked: "Regarding the three interpretations of 'single-mindedness without distraction' in the practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation), where does their meaning lie? He replied: "Being without distraction is one interpretation;

single-mindedness is another interpretation; and 'single-mindedness without distraction through nianfo' is yet another interpretation. This is according to the school of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight).
The Chan school’s exclusive cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to eliminate karmic afflictions is the teaching of "non-distraction.
